Why Owl Hoots at Night
Long ago, Owl was awake all day. He loved to talk, and his voice was very loud. Whenever Magpie began to sing, Owl hooted over the top of her song.
The other birds grew cross. They flew up high to the Sun and asked for help.
The Sun called Owl to the tallest tree. "The day belongs to the singers," said the Sun. "If you wish to hoot, you must wait until I sleep."
Owl grumbled, but he agreed. And that is why, even today, owls sleep in the daytime and hoot under the moon.

AnswerB: Magpie
AnswerC: the Sun

Long ago, the ancient Egyptians lived beside a mighty river called the Nile. All around them was dry, sandy desert.

ComprehensionText:
How a Scrape Heals
Seeing blood on your knee can be scary. But your body knows just what to do.
First, the blood at the top of the scrape gets thick and sticky. This is called a clot. It stops more blood from leaking out.
Next, the clot dries and turns into a hard, brown scab. The scab is like a tiny shield. Under it, your body is busy making new skin.
The scab may feel itchy, but try not to pick it. If you pull it off too early, the scrape can open again.
After a week or two, the scab falls off by itself. Pink, new skin is waiting underneath.
QuestionText: What happens straight after the blood gets thick and sticky?
AnswerB: new pink skin shows
AnswerC: the scrape starts to itch
AnswerD: the clot dries into a scab

How to Make a Friendship Bracelet
A friendship bracelet is a fun way to show a friend you care.
You will need:
three pieces of coloured wool, each as long as your arm
sticky tape
Steps:
1. Tie the three pieces together with a knot at one end.
2. Tape the knot to a table.
3. Plait the wool. Cross the left piece over the middle one, then the right piece over the middle one. Keep going.
4. When it fits around a wrist, tie another knot.
5. Give it to your friend with a big smile.
Tip: Choose your friend's favourite colours. They will know you were thinking of them!
QuestionText: How many pieces of wool do you need?
AnswerB: four
AnswerC: five

Under the shallow water in some bays, there are green meadows of seagrass. We must look after them!

Sadly, boat anchors and propellers can tear the seagrass out. It grows back very slowly.
Boaties, please drop your anchor on sand, not grass. Go slowly in shallow water. Let's keep the meadows green!

Mr Brown had a magnificent apple tree. On this hung five ripe, red apples.

Each day, Mr Brown went out to count the apples. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5! Five ripe, red apples.

One night, a tiny, grey mouse ran up the trunk of the tree. Tip, tap! Tip, tap!

She chewed through the stem of one apple.

Plop!

It fell to the ground where the mouse family was waiting. Nibble, nibble, nibble. The mouse family soon ate up every piece of the apple then scampered back home.

The next morning, Mr Brown came out of his house and counted the apples.

1, 2, 3, 4! Only four apples!

'A tall, tall thief must have come in the night and stolen my apple,' he said. He went back into his house, very puzzled.
QuestionText: At the end of the story, Mr Brown was puzzled because
AnswerA: he thought he had not counted the apples correctly.
AnswerB: he wondered why the thief had not taken all the apples.
AnswerC: he could not find the mouse family.
AnswerD: he was not sure how the apple had been taken.

ComprehensionText:
Front Seat, No Driver
On Saturday morning, Dad and Ivy caught the first train on the city's new metro line. Ivy raced to the very front carriage. Where the driver's cabin should have been, there was only a huge window.
'Who's driving?' Ivy whispered.
'Computers,' said Dad. 'They control the speed and the stops.'
Ivy gripped the rail. The train slid into the dark tunnel, and tiny green lights flicked past like fireflies. Soon Ivy let go of the rail and pressed her nose to the glass.
At each station, glass doors on the platform opened at the same moment as the train doors. 'Those stop people falling onto the tracks,' Dad explained.
Then the train rose out of the tunnel onto a tall bridge. The city spread out below them, and Ivy spotted the roof of her own school.
At the last stop, Ivy didn't move. 'Can we go back the same way?' she asked. 'I want to sit at the front again.'
QuestionText: What was at the front of the train where the driver's cabin would usually be?
AnswerB: a glass door
AnswerC: a computer screen

The Cereal Contraption
Ruby hated waiting for breakfast, so she decided to invent a machine to make it for her.
She spent all of Saturday building. A marble would roll down a ramp of books, knock over a line of dominoes and tip a cup that tugged a string. The string would tilt the cereal box over her bowl.
'It will never work,' said her brother Max, crunching his toast.
Ruby ignored him. She tested it once, and the marble flew off the ramp. She tested it again, and the dominoes fell the wrong way. By lunchtime, the kitchen floor was a sea of cornflakes.
Ruby swept up, moved the ramp and added a wall of pencils. On the tenth try, everything worked. The marble rolled, the dominoes clicked, the cup tipped and the cereal poured perfectly into the bowl.
Max stared with his mouth open. 'Can you make one for me?'
Ruby grinned. 'Sure,' she said. 'But first, who's going to pour the milk?'
QuestionText: In Ruby's machine, what did the string do?
AnswerB: knocked over the dominoes
AnswerC: rolled the marble

Albert Namatjira: Painter of the Ranges
Albert Namatjira was born in 1902 at Hermannsburg, west of Alice Springs. He was an Arrernte man, and as a boy he came to know every hill, creek and tree of his Country.
As a young man, Albert carved and decorated wooden objects to sell. Then, in 1936, an artist named Rex Battarbee came to paint the area. Albert offered to guide him to the best places in return for painting lessons. Rex showed him how to use watercolour paints.
Albert learned quickly. He painted the red cliffs of the MacDonnell Ranges, purple hills at sunset and tall white ghost gums that seem to shine against the sky.
In 1938, Albert held his first exhibition in Melbourne. Every painting sold. People across Australia had never seen the outback painted in such glowing colours.
Albert went on to paint hundreds of pictures. Today his works hang in galleries around the country, and members of his family still paint in his style.
QuestionText: Where did Albert hold his first exhibition?
AnswerB: in Alice Springs
AnswerC: in Hermannsburg

As a young man, Albert carved and decorated wooden objects to sell. Then, in 1936, an artist named Rex Battarbee came to paint the area. Albert offered to guide him to the best places in return for painting lessons. Rex showed him how to use watercolour paints.
Albert learned quickly. He painted the red cliffs of the MacDonnell Ranges, purple hills at sunset and tall white ghost gums that seem to shine against the sky.
In 1938, Albert held his first exhibition in Melbourne. Every painting sold. People across Australia had never seen the outback painted in such glowing colours.
Albert went on to paint hundreds of pictures. Today his works hang in galleries around the country, and members of his family still paint in his style.

AnswerA: Every painting sold at his first exhibition in Melbourne.
AnswerB: People across Australia had never seen the outback painted in such glowing colours.
AnswerC: Albert went on to paint hundreds of pictures.
AnswerD: Rex showed him how to use watercolour paints.

Sally Spangles was the popular young star of a TV show called Happy Families. She loved being recognised wherever she went. One day a new boy came into her class at school. Sally waited for him to ask for her autograph but he just said, 'Hi, I'm Melvin. What's your name?'

Sally was astounded. 'You mean you don't know who I am? Seriously?!' Melvin blinked at her through his large glasses. 'No, why should I?' 'Because I am the one and only Sally Spangles, star of Happy Families!' Melvin stared blankly at her. 'What's that?'

'Well, it's only one of the most popular shows on television!'

But Melvin simply shrugged his shoulders. 'Is that all? We don't have a TV at our place.'

By this time, a crowd of classmates had gathered. Surrounded by an audience, Sally instantly put on her standard act, pretending to faint. 'Quick, give me air!'

However, the rest of the class were so used to Sally's over-acting that they ignored her. They all stared at Melvin. Some gasped with disbelief, while others shook their heads with pity. A boy who didn't have a TV!!

Sally wasn't used to being ignored and she didn't like it. She glared at the newcomer but (annoyingly) Melvin stared straight back. 'Is that really so weird?' he asked mildly. 'Anyhow, I'd never have time to watch it.'

'Oh, I see! So what do you spend all your time doing then?' said Sally, her eyebrows raised.

Melvin blushed with embarrassment as he said, 'I'm guessing you don't play chess. Otherwise, you'd know that I'm the Melvin Preston: National Primary School Chess Champion!'
QuestionText: Why did Sally pretend to faint?
AnswerA: She was trying to be the centre of attention.
AnswerB: She wanted people to know she was unwell.
AnswerC: She was shocked that Melvin did not have a TV.
AnswerD: She wanted her classmates to move away from her.

Ironing Board surfing Charles had been looking forward to his summer vacation with his family. He was excited to go to the beach. His parents finally agreed to let his best friend Henry come along. Henry and Charles had been practicing their surfing on his mom's ironing board.

Despite the broken hinges and the goose egg on Henry's head, practicing had gone well. The six-hour drive to the beach passed quickly, as Charles and Henry had video game competitions. As they walked across the sand, they found themselves on strange beach they did not recognize. Charles' parents were nowhere in sight. There wasn't a single person on the beach.

"Whoa!" exclaimed Henry.

"What are we going to do?" moaned Charles.

AnswerA: It is heavier than a surf board.
AnswerB: It is not the right shape of the surf board.
AnswerC: The waves were too strong.

The Cloud Who Kept Her Rain
High above the plains floated a cloud named Nimbus. She was the biggest, fluffiest cloud in the sky, and she was very proud of it.
'If I let my rain fall, I will shrink,' she thought. 'Then nobody will admire me.' So she held on to every drop.
Down below, the grass turned brown and crisp. The creek shrank to a muddy trickle. The farmers looked up at Nimbus and sighed.
A little wind tugged at her edge. 'The land is thirsty,' it whispered. 'Your rain is not yours to keep.'
Nimbus puffed herself up even more. But her heavy load made her grumpy and grey, and soon nobody admired her at all.
At last, with a great rumble, she let go. Rain poured onto the fields. The creek gurgled back to life, and the grass turned green.
Nimbus was thin and pale now, but the farmers waved and children danced in the puddles. For the first time, Nimbus felt truly light.
QuestionText: Why did Nimbus hold on to her rain?
AnswerA: She was afraid she would shrink.
AnswerB: She was waiting for the wind.
AnswerC: She wanted the creek to dry up.
AnswerD: She was too high above the plains.

David built a special home for them, with a pond and a winding burrow. He fed his pair of platypuses, Jack and Jill, hundreds of worms and yabbies. Then, in 1943, something amazing happened. A baby platypus was born! It was named Corrie, and it was the first platypus ever bred in captivity.
Later, David moved to Queensland and opened his own wildlife park. He worked hard to protect animals and to teach people about them. Today, the park still carries his name.

The Toast Mystery
Have you ever dropped a piece of buttered toast? If you have, it probably landed butter side down, making a sticky mess on the floor. Many people think this is just bad luck, but scientists say there is a simple reason.
When toast slides off a plate or the edge of a table, it starts to spin as it falls. A kitchen table is not very high, so the toast only has time to make about half a turn before it hits the floor. The toast started with the butter facing up, so half a turn flips it over and the butter faces down. Splat!
Some people have tested this by dropping toast again and again. It landed butter side down much more often than butter side up.
If tables were much taller, the toast would have time to spin all the way round. But nobody wants a table taller than a grown-up!
So how can you save your snack? The best plan is to hold your plate carefully with both hands. Or you could just eat your toast quickly!

AnswerB: on its edge
AnswerC: on the table

I was lying in bed, reading, when I heard an odd scratching sound at the door.

I sighed. I put my book aside and went to open it. There was my little sister, Bonita, down on the ground on all fours. She looked up at me, opened her mouth and made a long, loud squeaking sound instead of saying my name, James.

I told her to go and bother someone else but she just stared. Then she scuttled past me and hid under my bed. She was amazingly quick!

I bent down to see where she was. She was hiding against the wall, in the darkness. I asked her to come out but she shook her head and squeaked again.

Now, you might think this is very strange behaviour, but there is a reason for it. You see, Bonita really wants a guinea pig but Mum says she can't have one. So Bonita says that if she can't have a guinea pig, then she'll pretend to be one until Mum says yes.

So that's what she was doing under my bed. The only way I could get her to come out was by offering her a carrot. I dangled it in the air, and she followed me (crawling, of course) out the door, down the hallway and back to her own room. Phew! This has been going for three days now. I hope Mum says yes to a guinea pig soon, because my little sister is driving me crazy!
QuestionText: Bonita is acting like a guinea pig because
AnswerA: she wants her brother to play with her.
AnswerB: she wants to persuade her mother to buy her a guinea pig.
AnswerC: she wants to avoid being punished by her mother.
AnswerD: she wants her mother to buy her a guinea pig.

On a nearby cattail, his father's yellow head glowed in the sun. Both parents clucked nervously as they watched their last baby learn to fly.

The little bird blinked his dark eyes and looked around. He saw a world of green plants and sparkling water. He fluffed up his feathers. Then he flapped his wings again and gave a little push with his feet against the cattail stem. All of a sudden, something really special happened—off he went flying through the air! He wobbled as he flew across the edge of the farm pond and looked for a place to land. His toes grabbed a long thin willow branch that hung out over the water. But the branch sagged under his weight. He slipped off the end of it and plopped down into the pond!

Now the little bird's parents hopped around the cattails and called to their baby. But there was nothing they could do to help him. Then something special happened again. The little bird began to swim! He dipped his wing tips low into the water. As the young bird splashed his wings in the water, bright sparkling droplets showered on his head. The drops spilled over his back and soaked his last dry feathers.

The pond looked calm and quiet. But the baby blackbird wasn't the only animal in the water. And some of the creatures—big fish, bullfrogs, and snapping turtles—would eat little birds whenever they had the chance.

As the little bird struggled along toward shore, a female bass noticed the ripples he was making. Then the big fish saw tiny feet and wet, feathery wing tips coming toward her. She started to drift upward toward the struggling bird.

Where Surnames Come From
Most people have a first name and a family name, or surname. Long ago, many people had only one name. As villages grew bigger, there might be five men called John! People needed a way to tell them apart, so surnames began.
Some surnames came from jobs. A smith worked with metal, so a man who made horseshoes might be called John Smith. A baker baked bread, and a cooper made wooden barrels.
Other surnames came from places. Someone who lived near a hill might be called Hill, and someone who lived beside a brook, or small stream, might become Brook.
Many surnames simply mean 'son of'. Johnson was once John's son, and Peterson was Peter's son.
Today, children usually share a surname with one or both parents, so the name passes down through the family. Some families join two surnames with a hyphen.
Next time you hear a surname, think about the story it might tell!

Most people have a first name and a family name, or surname. Long ago, many people had only one name. As villages grew bigger, there might be five men called John! People needed a way to tell them apart, so surnames began.
Some surnames came from jobs. A smith worked with metal, so a man who made horseshoes might be called John Smith. A baker baked bread, and a cooper made wooden barrels.
Other surnames came from places. Someone who lived near a hill might be called Hill, and someone who lived beside a brook, or small stream, might become Brook.
Many surnames simply mean 'son of'. Johnson was once John's son, and Peterson was Peter's son.
Today, children usually share a surname with one or both parents, so the name passes down through the family. Some families join two surnames with a hyphen.
Next time you hear a surname, think about the story it might tell!

AnswerC: surnames came from jobs, places and fathers' names

Roads That Lasted
About two thousand years ago, the ancient Romans built one of the greatest road systems in history. Their roads stretched across Europe, North Africa and the Middle East.
Roman roads were built in layers, a bit like a giant sandwich. Workers first dug a deep trench. They filled the bottom with large stones, then added smaller stones and gravel. On top, they fitted flat paving stones tightly together.
The roads were also slightly curved, higher in the middle than at the edges. When it rained, the water ran off into ditches at the sides. This stopped puddles from forming and kept the road strong.
Roman builders liked their roads to be as straight as possible. That way, soldiers, traders and messengers could travel quickly from town to town. Along the way, tall stone markers called milestones showed how far it was to the next town.
Amazingly, some Roman roads are still used today.

ComprehensionText:
Drawing with Scissors
Henri Matisse was a French artist famous for his bold, bright paintings. He loved colour more than almost anything else.
In 1941, when Matisse was seventy-one, he became very ill and needed a big operation. Afterwards, he was too weak to stand at an easel for long. He spent much of his time in bed or in a wheelchair. Many people thought his life as an artist was over.
Matisse did not give up. He asked his helpers to paint large sheets of paper in brilliant colours. Then, holding a big pair of scissors, he cut out shapes such as leaves, stars, birds and swirling seaweed. His helpers pinned the shapes to the walls while Matisse told them exactly where each piece should go.
He called this 'drawing with scissors'. Some of his cut-outs grew so large that they covered whole walls. Today, these joyful works hang in famous galleries around the world, and many people think they are among his very best.
QuestionText: What did Matisse's helpers paint?
AnswerB: the walls of his room
AnswerC: his wheelchair and bed

ComprehensionText:
Have you ever heard someone sing, "Happy birthday to you . . . happy birthday to you . . ."? If so, you are hardly alone—millions of people sing that song every year, and the tune is one of the most familiar of any song in North America.

Ironically, it is not known who wrote it! The tune was written by two sisters, Patty and Mildred Hill, who were school teachers in the late 19th century. But their song had different words; instead of "happy birthday to you," the song ran "good morning to all." The two sisters would sing this ditty to their students each morning as school began. In 1924, the tune was published in a song book, which added the "happy birthday" lyrics as verse two. Today, the second verse of that song has become one of the best known tunes in the world—and nobody knows who wrote the words!
QuestionText: Why is it ironic that the author of the words to "Happy Birthday" is not known?
AnswerA: because almost everyone knows the song
AnswerB: because it shows how unjust life can be
AnswerC: because of modern copyright laws

How Animals Use Tools Tools are usually thought of as human inventions. But did you know that animals use tools to solve problems, too?

The chimpanzee, for example, uses grass stems to catch termites. This animal knows where these insects live. It pokes a stem into the termites' nest. Then it waits. Inside the nest, the termites crawl over the stem. The chimpanzee pulls out the termite-covered stem and licks it clean. This is a good meal for a chimpanzee.

Sometimes the chimpanzee has trouble locating water. When this happens, it often uses leaves as a tool. The chimpanzee pushes leaves into places that it cannot reach. The leaves soak up the water from these places. Then the chimpanzee chews on the leaves. Chimps have also been known to use sticks as digging tools.

The woodpecker finch is another animal that uses tools. It uses small sticks to pick insects out of tree bark. Another animal that uses tools is the sea otter. It uses rocks to crack open shellfish. Here is how. The otter places the rock on its chest. Then it holds the shellfish in its paws and bangs it against the rock. This cracks the shell open and allows the otter to eat the creature inside.

The green heron uses bait to catch fish, just as humans use bait on the end of a fishing pole. The heron does this by picking up a small object with its beak. It flies over the water and drops the object onto the surface. Beneath the water, fish see the object and swim toward it. The This chimpanzee uses a stick as a tool to dig for termites.

Some animals have uses for tools other than gathering food and water. Some use leaves to dab at wounds or to clean. Some even use twigs as toothpicks. A scientist named Benjamin Beck discovered that crows are very good at solving problems. One unusual crow that lived in Beck's lab ate dry food moistened with a little water. When people forgot to add water to the food, the bird used a cup and added its own water. The elephant is one of the most intelligent animals. Using its trunk as an arm, the elephant puts grass and branches together. It then uses this tool to swat flies. When needed, this tool can also be used as a back scratcher. Let's not forget the amazing bottle-nosed dolphins. These remarkable animals twist sea sponges around their snouts. Why? Dolphins hunt the ocean's bottom-dwellers. They use their snouts to turn up sediment and find food. Sometimes they scrape their snouts on sand, rocks, shells, and other objects. Covering their snouts with sponges helps them avoid scrapes, or worse still, stings from poisonous animals.

ComprehensionText:
We'd only lived in the street for a week when my mother sent me down to the corner shop on an errand. I'd already heard the horror stories about the shopkeeper. The kids from school called him Groucho.

That day, for the first time, I stepped from the bright warmth of the street into the musty, arctic gloom of the corner shop.

'What do you want, boy?' It wasn't so much a voice as the rumbling from a bottomless volcano.

A sharp thrill of panic spread through my body and in a rush, all the schoolyard stories came back to me. Two boys that Groucho had caught stealing a bar of chocolate now felt very ill whenever they saw or smelled chocolate. Without being seen, Groucho could sneak up on you like a vampire, floating silently from the other end of the shop. He'd just appear at your shoulder and ask what you were doing.

'My mother' was all I could manage to choke out.

I saw the ranks of milk inside the door of the tall fridge and with hands that felt like feet, I fumbled a bottle onto the counter and began tugging coins from my pocket. As my sweaty fingers grappled with the stubborn silver, I made the mistake of looking up.

Groucho was not so much clothed as swathed in odd rags and small blankets against the cold. They were grubby and stringy at the edges and looked as if he slept in them. He wore a strange old purple woollen cap that exactly matched the colour of his gigantic lumpy nose. The lines in his face were as deep as cracks in the pavement and his teeth jutted out at all angles like the stubs of yellow crayons. Although his eyes were a deep black, as he leaned down to stare at me, tiny glints of light danced and revolved like distant galaxies. The old hands that rested in front of him were the grimy claws of some prehistoric bird of prey.

I tried to place my money on the counter but I was already moving for the door. The coins jangled in the silence and I heard one make a butting roll and clang on the floor. I hit the door hard, forgetting it opened inward, then tore it back and burst into the sunshine clutching the milk against my pounding chest as I finally remembered to breathe.
QuestionText: How did the narrator feel when the shopkeeper spoke to him?
AnswerB: guilty
AnswerC: irritated

I took a photo of the dune ripples and another of the beach ripples. At home I put them side by side. They looked almost the same, as if the sea and the wind had been copying each other's handwriting.

Gran's Fifty-Year Postcard
Gran had kept the postcard on her fridge for fifty years. It showed a penguin standing on an iceberg, and on the back, in faded pencil, she had written: One day.
Now, wrapped in a borrowed red jacket, Lily stood beside Gran on the deck of the ship as it slid into a bay in Antarctica. The water was as still as glass. Icebergs drifted past like enormous white sculptures, some streaked with a blue so bright it seemed to glow.
'Look!' Lily pointed. On the shore, hundreds of Adélie penguins waddled and squabbled, their black backs shining.
Small rubber boats carried the passengers to the beach, because the ship was too big to go near the shore. The air was so cold that it stung Lily's nose, and the snow squeaked under her boots. A penguin hopped right past her, carrying a pebble in its beak.
'They build their nests from stones,' said the guide. 'Sometimes they steal them from their neighbours.'
Lily laughed and turned to tell Gran, but Gran wasn't laughing. She was standing quite still, her gloved hands pressed to her mouth, and her eyes were shining.
'Are you all right?' Lily asked.
Gran nodded but didn't speak for a long moment. Then she pulled the old postcard from her pocket and held it up beside the real penguins.
'Not one day any more,' she said softly. 'Today.'

AnswerB: slept soundly
AnswerC: fed their chicks

ComprehensionText:
Every Kid Needs a Pen Pal
Imagine opening your letterbox and finding an envelope covered in colourful stamps from a country you have never visited. Inside is a letter written just for you. I believe every primary school student should have a pen pal, and here is why.
First, a pen pal teaches you about the world. My pen pal, Hana, lives in a small town in Japan. From her letters I have learnt that her class cleans the school every afternoon and that she eats rice for breakfast. No textbook ever told me things like that.
Second, writing letters makes you a better writer. When you know a real person will read your words, you take more care with spelling and handwriting. My teacher says my writing has improved more this year than ever before.
Third, a pen pal teaches patience. A letter can take two weeks to arrive, and then you must wait again for a reply. In a world where messages fly back and forth in seconds, learning to wait is a useful skill.
Some people say pen pals are old-fashioned and that video calls are faster. That may be true, but a video call disappears when it ends. A letter can be kept in a shoebox and read again years later. I keep all of Hana's letters, and I have reread the first one so many times that the folds have gone soft.
So grab a pen and some paper. Your new best friend could be waiting on the other side of the world.

AnswerB: costing a lot of money
AnswerC: hard to understand

Three Knots Worth Knowing
A good camper carries a torch, a water bottle and a length of rope. But a rope is only as useful as the knots you can tie in it. Learn these three, and you will be ready for almost anything the bush throws at you.
The reef knot
The reef knot joins two ends of rope together. It is perfect for tying up a bundle of firewood or closing the top of a bag. To tie it, remember 'right over left, then left over right'. A reef knot lies flat and neat, but be careful: it can slip loose if it is pulled very hard, so never use it to hold anything heavy.
The bowline
The bowline (say 'BOH-lin') makes a loop at the end of a rope that will not shrink or slip, no matter how much weight hangs from it. Sailors have trusted it for hundreds of years. Best of all, even after holding a heavy load, a bowline is easy to undo.
The taut-line hitch
This clever knot is a tent's best friend. Tie it where a guy rope loops around a tent peg. It can slide along the rope to tighten or loosen it, yet it grips firmly when the rope is pulled. Ropes often stretch when they get wet, and a sagging tent can collect puddles on its roof overnight. With a taut-line hitch, you simply slide the knot to make the rope tight again.
Why not grab a piece of string tonight and start practising?

Before the Sun Comes Up
On a dairy farm, the working day starts long before most people wake. Many dairy farmers in Australia are out of bed by four o'clock in the morning, because cows need to be milked twice a day, at roughly the same times.
First, the farmer rounds up the herd from the paddock and walks the cows slowly to the milking shed. Cows that are rushed or frightened give less milk.
Inside the shed, where some farmers play soft music on a radio, each cow steps into her own bay. The farmer cleans the cow's teats, then attaches the milking cups, which gently draw out the milk through soft rubber linings.The milk flows through pipes into a large steel vat, where it is quickly chilled.
After milking, the cows head out to fresh pasture. Farmers move the herd to a different paddock every day or two. This gives the grass in the old paddock time to regrow, so the cows always have plenty of good food to eat.
Once a day, a tanker truck arrives to collect the milk from the vat and take it to a factory. There it is tested, packaged and sent to shops.
Dairy farming is hard work in every kind of weather, but it is the most rewarding job in the country. The next time you pour milk on your cereal, remember the early start that brought it to your table.

When Stories Come True
Science fiction writers imagine what the future might look like. Sometimes, their wild ideas turn out to be surprisingly close to the truth.
More than 150 years ago, the French writer Jules Verne described a trip to the Moon. In his story, the travellers launched from Florida, felt weightless in space and splashed down in the ocean on their return. About a hundred years later, real astronauts did almost exactly that.
In 1945, a young British writer named Arthur C. Clarke suggested placing machines high above Earth to send radio signals around the world. People thought it sounded far-fetched. Today, communication satellites carry television, phone calls and internet signals across the planet every second.
Even the word 'robot' came from fiction. It first appeared in a play written in 1920 by a Czech writer.
Some inventors say these stories inspired them. As a boy, Igor Sikorsky read a different Jules Verne novel, featuring a flying machine that could rise straight up into the air. He never forgot it. Decades later, he designed one of the first successful helicopters.
Of course, many predictions have not come true. We are still waiting for flying cars to fill our skies! But science fiction does something important. It encourages us to ask 'What if?' In my opinion, that question is the most exciting one there is.

Maria Montessori's Small Chairs
Maria Montessori was born in Italy in 1870. At a time when most girls were expected to stay at home, Maria wanted to study science. Some people made fun of her, but she refused to give up. In 1896, she became one of the first women in Italy to qualify as a doctor.
As a doctor, Maria worked with children who were struggling to learn. She watched them closely and noticed that they learned best when they could touch and move things with their hands, rather than sitting still and listening.
In 1907, Maria opened a school for young children in a poor part of Rome. She called it the Casa dei Bambini, which means 'Children's House'. Most classrooms then had heavy desks bolted to the floor in rows. Maria's classroom was different. She had small, light tables and chairs made that children could carry themselves. Shelves were low, so children could reach things without asking an adult.
Children chose their own activities, such as pouring water, building towers of blocks or tracing letters cut from sandpaper. Visitors were amazed to see three- and four-year-olds working quietly for long periods.
Maria spent the rest of her life travelling the world to share her ideas. Today, there are thousands of Montessori schools, and many other classrooms have child-sized furniture too.

AnswerB: fixed firmly
AnswerC: ran away quickly

The Comet's Promise
I am a comet, a snowball of dust,
far out where the cold planets roam.
I drift through the dark for a hundred long years,
but always I turn and come home.

Out past the giants with rings and with moons,
where sunlight is thin as a thread,
I sleep in the silence, as frozen as stone,
with nothing but stars overhead.

The Sun is a campfire I glimpse from afar,
a spark at the edge of the night.
It tugs at my coat with an invisible string
and reels me back into the light.

As I rush ever closer, my ice starts to melt,
and I steam like a pot on the boil.
A tail made of glitter streams out at my back,
a long, ghostly ribbon uncoiled.

My tail always points away from the Sun,
whichever direction I race,
as though a great wind from the Sun's glowing heart
were blowing the hair from my face.

On a planet of blue, little faces look up
and point at the streak in the sky.
I wish I could stay and say hello to them all,
but I only have time to fly by.

So I swing round the Sun and race out again,
my tail drifting after like smoke.
Remember my face, little planet of blue,
and the night that I passed and you woke.

The children who wave at me now will be old
when I come back this way once again,
so tell all their grandchildren, 'Look to the sky!'
for I promise that I'll see them then.

AnswerB: a single night
AnswerC: ten years

Keep Cars on the Ground
Every few years, someone promises that flying cars are just around the corner. Videos show shiny machines zooming between skyscrapers. It looks thrilling, but I believe filling our skies with flying cars would be a big mistake.
Imagine it is the year 2075. Ten-year-old Priya steps outside her front door. Above her, hundreds of flying cars buzz like a swarm of angry bees. She cannot hear the birds or even her own thoughts. Her little brother covers his ears and refuses to walk to school. This is the noisy future we could be choosing.
Noise is only the first problem. A car with a flat tyre can pull over to the side of the road. A flying car with a broken engine has nowhere to go but down. Every driver would need far more training than drivers need today, and even skilled pilots make mistakes.
Flying cars would also use huge amounts of energy. Lifting a heavy vehicle into the air takes much more power than rolling it along a road. That means more batteries, more fuel and more harm to our planet.
Supporters say flying cars would end traffic jams. But the sky would soon fill up too, and a jam a hundred metres up is far more dangerous than one on the ground.
Instead of wasting billions on flying cars, let's build better trains, safer bike paths and quieter streets. The future should be calm, clean and safe, not buzzing over our heads.
QuestionText: Which reason does the writer give to show that flying cars would harm the planet?
AnswerA: Flying cars would be too noisy for birds.
AnswerB: Drivers would need much more training.
AnswerC: Lifting a vehicle takes more power than rolling it.
AnswerD: Engines could break down in the air.

Nobody Held the Pen
The bees build rooms with six straight sides
and share each waxy wall,
a golden city, packed so tight
there's not a gap at all.
And nobody held the pen.

The snail's shell is a winding stair
that circles round and in;
it starts out wide, then turns and turns
and tightens to a pin.
And nobody held the pen.

A pebble dropped into the pond
sends rings that ripple out,
each circle wider than the last,
a whisper grown to a shout.
And nobody held the pen.

A snowflake lands upon my glove
with six arms, lacy-white,
each one a copy of the rest,
then melts before my sight.
And nobody held the pen.

A spider spins a silver wheel
of spokes and rings so fine,
each gap the same from hub to edge,
each thread a perfect line.
And nobody held the pen.

The sunflower packs its face with seeds
in spirals, row on row,
some curving left and some curving right,
like whirlpools as they grow.
And nobody held the pen.

The gum leaf has a map of roads
that branch from one thick vein,
like creeks seen from an aeroplane
across a dusty plain.
And nobody held the pen.

The wind combs ridges on the dunes
in long and wavy bands,
as even as the lines I trace
with fingers through the sand.
And nobody held the pen.

I use a ruler for my lines,
a compass for my rounds,
and still I rub out half of them
with grumbling, scratchy sounds.
So who was holding the pen?

AnswerA: a different pattern found in nature
AnswerB: the same pattern in a different season
AnswerC: a different tool used for drawing
AnswerD: a different animal building a home

ComprehensionText:
Nobody Held the Pen
The bees build rooms with six straight sides
and share each waxy wall,
a golden city, packed so tight
there's not a gap at all.
And nobody held the pen.

The snail's shell is a winding stair
that circles round and in;
it starts out wide, then turns and turns
and tightens to a pin.
And nobody held the pen.

A pebble dropped into the pond
sends rings that ripple out,
each circle wider than the last,
a whisper grown to a shout.
And nobody held the pen.

A snowflake lands upon my glove
with six arms, lacy-white,
each one a copy of the rest,
then melts before my sight.
And nobody held the pen.

A spider spins a silver wheel
of spokes and rings so fine,
each gap the same from hub to edge,
each thread a perfect line.
And nobody held the pen.

The sunflower packs its face with seeds
in spirals, row on row,
some curving left and some curving right,
like whirlpools as they grow.
And nobody held the pen.

The gum leaf has a map of roads
that branch from one thick vein,
like creeks seen from an aeroplane
across a dusty plain.
And nobody held the pen.

The wind combs ridges on the dunes
in long and wavy bands,
as even as the lines I trace
with fingers through the sand.
And nobody held the pen.

I use a ruler for my lines,
a compass for my rounds,
and still I rub out half of them
with grumbling, scratchy sounds.
So who was holding the pen?

ComprehensionText:
Bread on the Goldfields
It was 1853, and the Ballarat goldfields were a sea of canvas tents and muddy holes. Every morning, Tom's father climbed down into their shaft with a pick and a bucket, hoping today would be the lucky day.
Tom's job was to rock the cradle. He tipped buckets of dirt and water into the wooden box and rocked it back and forth, so that any heavy gold would sink to the bottom. Most days, all he found was mud and stones. His arms ached, and his boots were always soaked.
Meanwhile, Tom's mother had an idea of her own. She built a clay oven behind their tent and began baking bread. The warm smell drifted across the diggings, and soon tired miners were lining up with coins in their hands. Some even paid with tiny flakes of gold.
One evening, Father climbed out of the shaft, empty-handed again. He sank onto a log with his head in his hands. Mum said nothing. She simply fetched the old tin box where she kept the bread money and tipped it onto the table. Coins and gold flakes spilled across the wood, glittering in the lamplight.
Father stared. Then he began to laugh.
'All this time I've been digging for gold,' he said, 'and you've been baking it.'
The next morning, Tom didn't rock the cradle. He chopped wood for the oven instead, whistling as he worked.
QuestionText: What was Tom's job at the start of the story?
AnswerB: baking the bread
AnswerC: digging the shaft

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
Carl sat chewing, his glasses balanced on the very tip of his nose. He was concentrating very hard. Cass watched fascinated. One more chew and they would slip off. "Well," Carl lifted his head and his glasses slid back into place. "I don't know if we can do anything more, Cass. If adults can't stop them, what can we do?"

The twins ate in silence, watching the sun slip behind the distant skyline, silhouetting the tall faceless office blocks that poked out of a shifting yellow haze. The din of the city traffic barely reached them. It mingled with the warm shushing sound of the surrounding park.

The Trumper Tree rose above them, majestic and tall, its twisted branches and gnarled trunk swirling in strange patterns. It looked as if it reached into the sky forever.

"I'm going to save a leaf from the Trumper Tree as a memento," said Cass and she picked up a fallen leaf. "Here's one for you," and she handed it to Carl. He was very quiet. The air became heavy and still. The park seemed to be holding its breath.

"Let's make a wish, a wish to make things right," whispered Cass.

"I don't believe in wishes," was Carl's reply, but he didn't push the leaf away; he placed it carefully in his pocket.

Around them the valley waited, motionless and silent. Cass shivered. "I feel strange, eerie. I can almost hear the tree speaking to me."

"What am I supposed to listen for?"

"Quiet! Can't you hear? There's a sound in the leaves, a sort of stirring, a movement, a rustling."

"And for your next trick there'll be gnomes in the grass." Carl was not impressed.

Cass was listening intently. "It's saying that now is the time, now is special, if we wish now something important will happen."

"And pigs might fly. Come on Cass, it's time we went home."

"Please let's try one wish now. Come on Carl, please...!"

"Oh, all right. Just one, then we must go or Mum and Dad will be late for that meeting."

"Let's put our arms around the tree and wish hard for something to save it."

AnswerB: hiding from his parents
AnswerC: quickly finishing a big meal

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
The latest Tyranno movie, Tyranno 2: Earth defence, has just taken a nosedive and crash-landed at a cinema near you all in 3D! While the original Tyranno was a visual feast with strong characters and a gripping story, Tyranno 2 has failed miserably as so many sequels do. It is loosely based on the second book in the excellent series by Lillian Sidle, but it has mutated into a truly awful movie. In particular, parts of the plot which were significant in the book have been left out of the script. This plot-thinning has had the effect of creating characters that are somewhat one-dimensional even if they look great in their dinosaur costumes.

Simon Gray, who did such a fabulous job in the first movie, plays Tyro. He is responsible for defending Earth from the evil pirate dinosaur Piratopod. Help with this mission is provided by a couple of velociraptor co-stars named Barry (Evan Green) and Kevin (Brian Scott). Piratopod has invented a solar-powered meteor magnet and intends to capture meteors from their space orbits, re-directing them onto a collision course with Earth. Tyro must mobilise the Earth Defence Team to locate and disable Piratopod's secret weapon. It's a typical 'good-guy-fights-bad-guy-and-overcomes-a-few-problems-along-the-way-while-winning-in-the-end' sort of movie. Usually this is a reasonable formula for success. However, the plot is mind-numbingly predictable, with gaps in the story that become obvious quite early on. This also means that the story tends to jolt strangely from one scene to the next.

I often use a 'spoiler alert' to warn readers when I intend to provide key details about a movie. In this case however, the story is so under-developed that there aren't many key details to reveal. You would think the director might have considered borrowing ideas from Sidle's books to make the characters more interesting - for instance Piratopod's twisted personality was actually explained as the result of traumatic events in his past. But no.

It is clearly in special effects that all the time and energy were invested in this movie, and if you love this sort of thing you will be enthralled. The views of Earth and the Moon are spectacular. I wasn't sitting in a cinema wearing 3D glasses; I was out there in space! Although the story is weak and the characters under-developed, the special effects are brilliant. They are the icing on a stale cake!

If the movie makers had followed Lillian Sidle's work more closely, this movie could have been a success. My suggestion to fans is to save your money on this movie and buy the book instead.

Reviewed by Lee Evan
Rated: PG

AnswerA: This is how the characters are portrayed in the book.
AnswerB: The actors did not have the experience to play the parts.
AnswerC: There is a lack of character development in the movie.
AnswerD: The characters are played by unknown actors in the movie.

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
Windows into the Wild
Walk into many natural history museums and you will find glass cases that seem to open onto another world: a misty rainforest, a snowy mountain slope or a billabong at sunset. These scenes are called dioramas. Although each one looks like a window, it is really a clever illusion built by a team of artists and scientists.
Creating a diorama usually happens in several stages.
First, the team studies the real place. Artists visit the location, take photographs, make sketches and collect samples of soil, leaves and rocks. Scientists check which animals and plants really belong together, and at what time of year.
Next, a painter creates the background on a curved wall at the back of the case. Because the wall curves, there are no corners to give the trick away. Distant hills and sky are painted in soft, pale colours, since faraway things look hazy to our eyes.
Then the foreground is built. This is the part closest to the glass. It holds real or carefully copied rocks, logs and soil, along with model leaves made one by one from wax, paper or plastic. Some dioramas contain thousands of handmade leaves.
The hardest job is joining the two parts. Where the real ground meets the painted wall, the colours and shapes must match exactly. If they do, visitors cannot tell where the solid ground ends and the painting begins.
Finally, preserved animals or lifelike models are put in place, and the lighting is set. Lights hidden above the case can make a scene look like early morning or late afternoon.
Some visitors today prefer screens and touch displays, and a few museums have removed their older dioramas. Yet many people still stand at the glass for minutes at a time. A good diorama lets you see an animal in its home, all in a single glance, in a way that a label or a photograph never could.
QuestionText: Why is the background painted on a curved wall?
AnswerA: so the lights can be hidden behind it
AnswerB: so more animals can fit inside the case
AnswerC: so there are no corners to give the trick away
AnswerD: so visitors can see it from both sides

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
On the Tip of My Tongue
A quiz kid called Lachlan McRae
Knew the answer but just couldn't say.
It was there on his tongue,
Like a bell left unrung,
And it came to him later that day.
You know the feeling. You are trying to remember the name of a film, a song or the kid who sat next to you in Year 2. You might even know that it starts with 'M' or has three syllables, but the word itself refuses to come out. Scientists have a name for this everyday mishap. They call it a tip-of-the-tongue moment.
In 1966, two researchers at Harvard University decided to study it. They read out dictionary definitions of rare words, such as 'sampan', and asked students to name each word. Many students got stuck partway. Often they could guess the first letter, or they came up with words that sounded similar, like 'Siam' and 'sarong'. This showed that the brain had found part of the word, but not all of it.
Since then, studies have found that most people have a tip-of-the-tongue moment about once a week. These moments become more common as people get older, and they happen most often with names.
So what should you do when a word gets stuck? Strangely, trying harder can make things worse, because your brain keeps landing on the wrong word. Many experts suggest thinking about something else. The missing word often pops up on its own, sometimes hours later, usually at a moment when it is no help at all.
My uncle Dev learned this the hard way. At a trivia night, his team needed one last answer: the name of the longest river in Australia. Dev was sure he knew it. He scrunched up his face, drummed on the table and muttered 'Mur... Mur...' until the time ran out. His team lost by one point. Halfway home in the car, he suddenly shouted 'The Murray!' so loudly that Aunty Mel nearly dropped her phone. He still blames the trivia host.

AnswerB: light-hearted and informative
AnswerC: angry and complaining

The Same Shape Twice
Lena's art teacher had asked the class to draw 'a pattern found in nature', and by Saturday morning Lena still had a blank page. Half the class had already done zebra stripes. Spider webs were too fiddly.
'Come up Tawny Hill with me,' said Grandpa, lacing his boots. 'Patterns are easier to find when you stop looking so hard.'
The track was steep and dusty. Halfway up, Lena picked up a fallen gum leaf. A pale line ran down its middle, and thinner lines branched off it, then split again and again until they were as fine as hairs. She tucked it into her sketchbook without thinking much about it.
At the top, they sat on a flat rock. Far below, the creek wound across the flats towards the sea. Near the coast it split into two channels, then four, then a dozen silver threads that spread out like the fingers of a hand dipping into the water.
Lena frowned. Something about it tickled her memory. She opened her sketchbook, and the gum leaf slid out onto the rock. She held it up against the view. The thick middle vein, the branches, the tiny threads at the edges: the creek was drawing the very same shape across the land.

ComprehensionText:
Amphibian Population Declining:

Scientists Concerned What's happening to the world's frogs, toads, and other amphibians? Amphibians are cold-blooded, and they tend to live near water. Thousands of species of amphibians live all over the world. But studies show that their numbers have declined very suddenly. Hundreds of species now face extinction. Scientists aren't sure why this is happening, but they are worried. They fear that it may signal trouble that could affect other living things on Earth, including people.

Some scientists blame pesticides for these problems. Farmers use these poisons to keep bugs from eating their crops. Amphibians have very thin skin. They absorb poisons quickly. Pesticides cause problems with the way frogs develop. For example, the back legs of some frogs do not grow long enough. Their short legs make it hard for them to swim. Also, some frogs can't breed. Fewer babies mean fewer frogs.

Amphibians are also disappearing, though, in places where pesticides are not used. Some people blame the problem on loss of habitat. For example, people have been cutting down the rain forests in South America for the past 25 years. The amphibians that once lived there now have no place to live. Amphibians have also been forced out by cities and towns. As more people move into an area, they use up more of the land.

Pollution may also be hurting amphibians. Air pollution allows more radiation from the sun to reach Earth. Once again, amphibians' thin skin hurts them. The radiation gets through their skin more easily than it does the skin of other animals.

Scientists warn that big problems with the environment would affect amphibians first. Because of this, the death of so many amphibians is like a red flag to the rest of us. We must figure out what is killing Earth's amphibians before it's too late.

AnswerA: They cause the frogs' skin to become thinner.
AnswerB: They change the way that frogs behave.
AnswerC: They cause frogs to develop abnormally.
AnswerD: They damage the brains of baby frogs.

Ludwig Van Beethoven Reading Comprehension Name ____ Ludwig Van Beethoven is widely considered the most influential composer in history. Born in 1770, during the height of Mozart and Haydn's popularity, Beethoven's music is what we now think of as the bridge between the Classical period (ca. 1750-­1800) and the Romantic period (ca. 1800-­1900). The impact he had on the composers that came after him is immeasurable. As a young adult, Beethoven moved to Vienna, Austria, with the hopes of being Mozart's composition student. Unfortunately, he was too late, so he studied with Franz Joseph Haydn instead. During this time, Beethoven's music was very reflective of Haydn and Mozart's work, while still maintaining originality.

Then, in 1802, Beethoven came upon an earth-­shattering realization – the deafness he was experiencing, and hoped was temporary, was permanent. As a musician, one's hearing is arguably the most important thing to have. Imagine composing something and not being able to hear it! Beethoven retreated to the countryside in Austria, to a place called Heiligenstadt, where he wrote the now famous Heiligenstadt Testament. This was a letter to his brother in which he described his crossroads: he could give up, or he could overcome. In addition to his loss of hearing, Beethoven suffered from incapacitating abdominal pain. His devoted group of friends often competed with each other to take care of him as his suffering intensified. The premiere of his third Symphony in 1803 revealed which option he chose. The response was gigantic – the Western world was stunned and excited by such a new sound. The opening features the melody in the cellos rather than the usual violins. Furthermore, the duration of the piece was more than double a typical Haydn symphony – almost one hour! This expansive form allowed for unexpected, dramatic harmonies to unfold, telling a story of a hero's struggle and triumph.

Nicknamed the Eroica, Beethoven originally dedicated this symphony to Napoleon Bonaparte, who he saw as a hero of his time. Like the founding fathers of the United States, Beethoven supported the ideals of the Enlightenment, such as individualism and personal freedom. Once Napoleon declared himself Emperor, Beethoven famously scratched out Napoleon's dedication. Beethoven arguably proved himself to be the true hero of the story. Not only did he hold fast to his progressive beliefs, but he also exhibited personal struggle and triumph in his monumental accomplishment through his growing deafness. Breaking norms was natural for Beethoven. Throughout his life, he expressed disdain for authority and was said to cut piano performances short if members of the audience were chattering or failed to give their full attention.

After the Eroica, and eventually the Ninth symphony, containing the famous "Ode to Joy" chorus, most composers tried to model their music after Beethoven's. His individualism sparked a revolution in classical music;; history would never be the same!
QuestionText: Which of the following best describes Beethoven's early work?
AnswerA: Totally original and revolutionary for its time
AnswerB: Unoriginal;; but similar to the styles of popular composers of the time
AnswerC: Original and different from the styles of popular composers of the time
AnswerD: Original;; but similar in style to Mozart and Haydn

Books the Size of a Matchbox
In 1826, in a stone house on the edge of the wild Yorkshire moors in England, four children received a present that would change their lives. Their father brought home a box of twelve wooden toy soldiers for Branwell, the only boy. Before long, his sisters Charlotte, Emily and Anne had each claimed a soldier of their own.
The Bronte children had already known sadness. Their mother had died when they were very young, and two older sisters had died too. Their aunt had moved in to help run the household, but the children spent many hours entertaining themselves. They had few friends nearby, so they turned to each other.
The soldiers soon came alive in their imaginations. The children gave them names, adventures and whole kingdoms to rule. Together they invented an imaginary land called Glass Town, with its own cities, newspapers and quarrels.
Then they began writing the stories down. Because the books were meant to be read by the toy soldiers, the children made them tiny. Some were only about five centimetres tall, smaller than a matchbox. They stitched the pages together by hand and filled them with writing so minute that it is hard to read without a magnifying glass. Paper was expensive, so every scrap of space was used.
As they grew older, Emily and Anne broke away to create their own imaginary kingdom, called Gondal, while Charlotte and Branwell kept writing about Glass Town. Their games lasted well into adulthood.
Those hours of play were like a training ground. All three sisters went on to become famous novelists. Charlotte wrote Jane Eyre, Emily wrote Wuthering Heights and Anne wrote Agnes Grey. Branwell became a painter.
Today, some of the tiny books are kept in museums. Visitors peer at the handwriting and imagine four children by the fire, building whole worlds together out of a simple box of soldiers.

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
Ten Minutes Before Maths
A report by the Year 5 Student Council, Kurrajong Primary School
Purpose
In Term 2, the Student Council suggested a ten-minute fitness break before maths each morning. We believed that moving our bodies would help students concentrate. The principal agreed to a four-week trial in the three Year 5 classes. This report describes what happened.
What we did
Each morning at 9.50, classes went to the basketball court. Student leaders took turns running the session, which included star jumps, skipping, a short jog and a stretching cool-down. On wet days, classes did seated stretches inside instead.
What we found
At the end of the trial, we surveyed all 72 Year 5 students. Fifty-one said they enjoyed the breaks, twelve said they did not mind them, and nine said they would rather stay inside. Teachers noticed that students settled into maths more quickly on most days.
Many students wrote comments. 'I used to feel sleepy by the time maths started, but now I'm wide awake and ready to go,' wrote Priya from 5B. Jonah from 5C wrote, 'The jog made me so puffed that my hand shook when I tried to write.'
We also noticed some problems. On cold mornings, frost glittered on the court and the icy air nipped at our fingers, so some students were slow to warm up. The trial also took ten minutes from each maths lesson, and one teacher said her class did not finish its work on two days.
Recommendation
The Student Council strongly recommends that the fitness break continue for all classes from Year 3 to Year 6. We believe the benefits clearly outweigh the small problems. On very cold days, we suggest moving the break into the hall.

AnswerA: Nine students said they would rather stay inside.
AnswerB: Student leaders took turns running the sessions.
AnswerC: Fifty-one of the 72 students said they enjoyed them.
AnswerD: Classes did seated stretches inside on wet days.

What she saw first was a moving shadow. In the trees that bordered the meadow, among their dark trunks, something moved. She heard nothing to alarm—not over the rush of water and the sweep of wind—but she saw a dark, crouched shape moving. The shadow, no more than a darker darkness in the night, crept out from the mass of trees, crept low across the long grass towards the docking place. No man of the village would move so. A man of the village, come out to check a hastily secured boat, would carry a light. He would come along the path that ran from the village through the Innyard, the path she stood on. No fisherman would be setting off, not at this hour, not on a moonless night when all the stars shining together couldn't penetrate the dark, windy air.

Birle stood motionless, watching. She herself ought not to be out in the night. Da and Nan would not be pleased to know how she had left her small sisters asleep in the bed they shared, pulled on her skirt and overshirt, and latched the door stealthily behind her to tiptoe past the room where her brothers slept, past the room where Da and Nan slept, down the broad staircase and across the empty public room. In the kitchen, where the banked fire glowed in its ashes, she had put on her boots and taken her cloak from its hook. The dogs, if they heard anything, knew her steps and took no alarm. Da and Nan, if they knew, would be mightily displeased, and they would lay angry words across her shoulders. Aye, they were counting the days left to the spring fair, when they would have her married and gone from their care. Aye, and Birle was counting them too.

The shadow was human, she had no doubt of that. Only a man or woman would move so, hunched over, gliding along the edge of the river like a beast on the hunt among the long grasses. Watching, Birle let the wind urge her down the path to the docking place. Whatever else, the shadow was up to nothing lawful.

Soaking spring rains had turned the path to mud. Her boots made squishing sounds, so she stepped off the path into the grass. As soundlessly as the shadow before her, but more swiftly, she approached the river.

She should return to the sleeping Inn, she knew that, and rouse her brothers. At the least, she should turn and call out an alarm, to set the dogs barking. But the mystery of the intruder, like the mystery of the night which had called her from sleep, kept her from doing what she ought.

AnswerA: not have been holding a light.
AnswerB: not have been out in the wind.
AnswerC: have been carrying fishing gear.

The First Lighthouse

It was in ancient Egypt, around 2300 years ago, that the great Pharaoh Ptolemy I Soter ordered plans to be drawn up for what was to be the world's first lighthouse. It was to be built on the island of Pharos, one-and-a-half kilometres off the coast of the city of Alexandria. The purpose of the Lighthouse of Pharos, as it became known, was to protect ships coming into the dangerous waters of the Alexandria harbour. Standing more than 110 metres high and built out of white marble, the Lighthouse of Pharos was so impressive that it became one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

In those days, as nearly the tallest building around, it must have had the best views in the world! (The pyramids at Giza were taller, but it was forbidden to climb them—as it still is now.)

The design of the lighthouse was very different to those we see today; it was built in three stages. The bottom level was over 60 metres high and more than 30 metres square. It looked like a huge box. On top of the box was an octagonal tower about 27 metres high with each of its eight sides more than 18 metres wide. And on top of the tower was a cylinder over seven metres high. During the day, the sun reflected off mirrors made of highly-polished bronze and at night, the lighthouse was lit by fires. It was said that the light from the Lighthouse of Pharos could be seen for more than 56 kilometres out to sea.

Incredibly, almost 700 years after it collapsed in an earthquake, the fame of the Lighthouse of Pharos lives on. In October 1994, Frenchman Dr Jean-Yves Empereur was asked by the Egyptian Supreme Council of Antiquities to investigate an area beneath the sea, just outside Alexandria's eastern harbour. In 1995 he took a team of divers, topographers, Egyptologists and photographers with him and started to mark, chart and illustrate approximately 1000 archaeological artefacts found on the bottom of the sea.

Apart from locating enormous blocks of stone and fragments from columns, the excavators also found sphinxes, parts of obelisks and inscribed blocks, all of which the excavators believed most likely belonged to the Lighthouse of Pharos. Even more exciting was the discovery that some of these building materials were much older than the Lighthouse of Pharos.

The Egyptian authorities are planning to build a modern version of the lighthouse on the very same spot at Pharos. This lighthouse will be made of concrete with glass walls and will be 145 metres high. The walls will reflect the sun by day and a beacon will cast its light at night.

The Gap in the Arch
All through the winter of 1930, Molly Fraser walked to the end of her street in North Sydney every afternoon to look at the bridge. For years it had been growing out from both sides of the harbour, two great steel arms reaching towards each other across the water. Each day the gap between them looked a little smaller.
Molly's father was a rigger on the bridge. He left before dawn and came home with grease on his hands and stories in his head. He told her about the creeper cranes that crawled along the top of each half-arch, lifting steel into place. He told her about the riveting gangs, too: one worker heated the rivets in a little furnace until they glowed, then tossed them through the air to a catcher who snatched them in a metal cup.
'What stops the two halves from falling into the harbour?' Molly asked one night.
'Cables,' said Dad. 'Huge steel cables anchored in tunnels in the rock. They hold each half back, like a hand on a dog's collar.'
In August, the workers began to let the cables out, slowly, a little each day. The two half-arches tilted forward, inch by careful inch. Half of Sydney seemed to be watching.
Then, late on the night of the nineteenth, the two halves touched. Molly heard the news from a neighbour running down the street, shouting. The next morning she raced to the corner. The ragged gap had gone. Instead, one enormous arch curved across the sky, steel grey against the blue, as if it had always been there.
That evening, Dad came home tired but smiling. Molly could hear the ships in the harbour hooting, and the clatter, clang and rattle of the riveters still working in the distance.
'Is it finished?' she asked.
'Not yet,' said Dad, ruffling her hair. 'But the hardest part is done. Now they can hang the road.'

The Bird Behind the Mud Wall
In the forests of Asia and Africa lives a bird with one of the strangest nesting habits on Earth. Hornbills are large birds with huge curved beaks, and many species have a hollow helmet called a casque on top. But it is what happens inside their nests that truly amazes scientists.
When it is time to lay her eggs, a female hornbill chooses a hollow in a tall tree. She climbs inside, and then she does something remarkable: she seals herself in. Using mud, chewed fruit and her own droppings, she plasters the entrance until only a narrow slit remains. In some species, her mate brings mud to help.
For the next few weeks, sometimes for several months, the female stays shut inside. In many species she sheds her flight feathers while she is there. She lays her eggs, keeps them warm and cares for the chicks when they hatch.
The wall works like a fortress. Snakes, monkeys and other hungry animals cannot reach the eggs through such a tiny gap. But it also means the female depends completely on her partner.
The male's task is exhausting. Day after day, he flies back and forth through the forest, collecting fruit, insects and small animals. He swallows the food, carries it to the nest, then brings it back up and passes it, piece by piece, through the slit to the female's waiting beak. A male may make dozens of trips in a single day. If something happened to him, his family would be in serious trouble.
When the chicks are larger and the nest is crowded, the female breaks out through the wall. In some species, the chicks then rebuild the seal by themselves and stay safely inside until they are ready to fly.
Sadly, many hornbills are now threatened because the giant trees they need are being cut down. Without old trees with big hollows, there is nowhere to build these remarkable mud-walled nurseries.

Dust by Charles Grayson

1 As Edwin rested his cheek against the side of his cow, Nelly, he could hear the wind whistling through the barn walls and see the air begin to darken with dust. Annie and Jewel were giggling as they played in the hayloft above him when one of the girls began to wheeze. Edwin quickly finished milking the cow and called to his sisters. "Hurry up, girls," he said, "another black blizzard is coming."

2 The wind suddenly picked up strength, and before Edwin's eyes, the farmhouse—only 50 feet away—became nearly invisible. Without hesitation, Edwin grabbed two pieces of heavy twine, tied one around each girl's waist, and then tied the two girls together. He took Annie's hand and instructed her to hold tightly to Jewel. Leaning into the blinding wind, Edwin slowly navigated them back to the house.

3 Inside, Ma was relieved to see the children. With a sigh, she took the milk from Edwin, eyeing the familiar dust that she would try to skim off before serving the milk to her family. Although it was early morning, the dust storm outside made the small farmhouse dark and dismal. Edwin slapped the dirt from his jacket with his hands. He was weary of the dust, too, but he was smiling inside because tomorrow his father was coming home.

4 The next morning dawned clear and calm. Edwin swept the house while his mother worked in the yard, rescuing her daffodils from the dust that had drifted against the foundation of the house like gritty snow. The clatter of a rundown automobile heralded the arrival of Edwin's father, and the boy raced outside.

5 The family gathered around Pa, who hugged each one of them tightly. He had been in Arizona for three weeks picking cotton. This spring the ground was hard and barren, and the constant dust storms made it impossible to cultivate crops. Pa had to find some way to earn money—his children were wearing tattered hand-me-downs, and his small herd of cattle was slowly starving.

Interim Assessment Unit 2

6 When Ma asked about the work, Pa said that the wages he earned were far less than what had been promised. Still, he'd brought home enough money to see them through another month. Eventually, the joy of being reunited with his family faded, and the careworn expression returned to Pa's face.

7 After Pa had been home a few days, Edwin overheard his parents having a serious discussion. "I just don't know if I can leave our home," Ma said, a note of grief in her voice. Pa had heard there was work on commercial farms in California, where cotton, oranges, and other crops grew nearly year round.

8 "I know it's not like owning our own farm, but what choice do we have?" Pa pleaded. Afterward, Ma went into the yard and stood for a long time by her beloved lilac bush, staring out at the desolate fields.

9 Later, Pa asked Edwin to ride the horse into town to purchase provisions. Edwin rode at a slow pace, thinking. He didn't like it when his parents argued, and he didn't like it when his father had to leave home to work. Most of all, Edwin wished there was something he could do to assist his family. At the store, he walked past the half-empty shelves to the back counter and asked Mr. Harburger for beans and flour.

10 As Edwin waited, something bright and orange caught his eye. It was an old advertisement on the shelf in front of him—a photograph of a glistening orange grove with the words "Sunny California" splashed across the top. Edwin had never seen an orange grove before. Studying the picture, Edwin's face brightened. "Take it," Mr. Harburger said with a wink. At home, Edwin tacked the picture up next to his bed. One day, Edwin even caught his mother examining the photograph of the orange grove, smiling for the first time in a long time.

11 When autumn arrived, Edwin's parents learned the government was offering to buy starving livestock for slaughter. Most farmers knew their animals could not survive another winter, so they accepted the offer in exchange for some much-needed cash. After a long discussion, Edwin's parents did the same. Edwin sensed a change was coming.

12 The cow Nelly remained, but Edwin could see that she was becoming desperately thin. The next day, Edwin sold Nelly at the Baileys' farm. The Baileys were doing better than most folks, though Edwin couldn't say why. He returned home with 16 dollars in his pocket and a little relief knowing that Nelly would be cared for.

13 Later that evening, Edwin's parents made an important announcement: they would be packing whatever would fit into their old automobile and moving to California. Then Edwin made his own announcement. "Here," he said, handing his father the 16 dollars. "We can buy fuel with this!" Interim Assessment Unit 2
QuestionText: Based on the passage, how do Ma's feelings about moving change over time?
AnswerA: She becomes more and more resistant to the idea of moving.
AnswerB: She grows more comfortable with the idea of moving.
AnswerC: She likes the idea of moving initially, then comes to dislike it.
AnswerD: She becomes more confident that the family should not move.

The Slowest Job in the World
The bone was smaller than my hand, and I had been working on it for three days.
'Patience, Mia,' said Aunt Leonie, without looking up from her own workbench. 'That rock has been sitting there for a hundred million years. It can wait another afternoon.'
I adjusted my magnifying lamp and went back to scraping. The tool I was using looked like a dentist's pick. Each stroke removed a crumb of grey stone no bigger than a grain of sugar. Around me, the fossil laboratory hummed with the sound of fans and the quiet tapping of volunteers bent over their own blocks of rock.
It had all started two weeks earlier, at the dig site on a sheep station west of town. The ground there was cracked and bare, and heat shimmered off it in waves. We had spent most of the morning finding nothing but pebbles. Then, just before lunch, I noticed a dark, glossy edge poking out of the dirt near my boot. I almost walked past it. When Aunt Leonie saw it, she went very still, then knelt and brushed away the soil with her fingers.
'Well done,' she said softly. 'That's bone.'
The block of rock was wrapped in plaster, like a broken arm, and carried back to the laboratory on the back of a truck. I had imagined that we would simply crack it open and pull out a skeleton. Instead, Aunt Leonie handed me the pick and showed me how to remove the rock one tiny flake at a time.
Now, on the third afternoon, something changed. As I brushed away the dust, a smooth curve appeared, then a ridge, then a row of tiny pits along the surface. I held my breath.
'Aunt Leonie,' I whispered. 'I think it's a joint.'
She came over and leaned in close to the lamp. For a long moment she said nothing. Then she smiled, wider than I had ever seen her smile.
'It's the end of a toe bone,' she said. 'Do you know what that means? Where there's one toe, there might be a foot. And where there's a foot . . .'
She didn't need to finish. I looked down at the little grey bone, and suddenly three days didn't seem slow at all. It seemed like the beginning of something.
I picked up my tool and leaned closer to the lamp.
QuestionText: Why did Aunt Leonie tell Mia to be patient?
AnswerA: The laboratory was about to close for the day.
AnswerB: The work of uncovering the bone could not be rushed.
AnswerC: Mia was making too much noise with her tool.
AnswerD: The bone was likely to crack in half at any moment.

Pack a Beanie: The Case for Winter Camping
Ask most Australian families when they go camping, and they will say the summer holidays. It makes sense. The days are long, the weather is warm and school is out. But I believe that families who pack away their tents when the weather cools are missing out on the best camping of the year. It is time to give winter camping a chance.
First, consider the crowds, or rather the lack of them. In January, popular campgrounds are booked out months ahead. Tents are squeezed together so tightly that you can hear your neighbours snoring. In June or July, many of those same campgrounds are almost empty. You can choose the best site, wander along quiet tracks and hear nothing at night but the wind in the trees.
Second, winter is often more comfortable than summer. Anyone who has tried to sleep in a tent on a 35-degree night knows how miserable it can be. In many parts of Australia, winter days are mild and sunny, perfect for long walks without the risk of heatstroke. There are fewer flies and mosquitoes to battle, too. When the temperature drops after dark, a good sleeping bag and a woolly beanie will keep you snug.
Third, winter brings experiences that summer simply cannot offer. With fire restrictions often eased in the cooler months, many campgrounds allow campfires, where families can gather to talk, cook and toast marshmallows. Long, dark nights mean you can see the stars well before bedtime. On a clear winter night, away from city lights, the Milky Way spills across the sky like a river of sugar.
Some people will argue that winter camping is too cold and too wet. It is true that you need to be prepared. Pack warm layers, a waterproof jacket and a tent that can handle rain, and always check the weather forecast before you leave. But a little preparation is a small price to pay. After all, as the saying goes, there is no such thing as bad weather, only the wrong clothes.
So this winter, don't let your tent gather dust in the garage. Pack your beanie, grab your thermos and head outdoors. You may find that the coldest season gives you the warmest memories.

AnswerA: The days are too short for long walks.
AnswerB: Most walking tracks are closed to visitors.
AnswerC: Tents often leak during summer storms.
AnswerD: Campgrounds are crowded and booked out early.
