ComprehensionText:
The Man Behind Mother Goose
Most people know the stories of Cinderella, Puss in Boots and Sleeping Beauty. Far fewer know the name of the man who first wrote them down in the form we recognise today. His name was Charles Perrault, and for most of his long life, fairy tales were the last thing anyone expected from him.
Perrault was born in Paris in 1628, the youngest son of a well-off family. He was a clever, confident student who once walked out of school after arguing with his teacher, and then taught himself by reading at home with a friend. Later he trained as a lawyer, although he did not stay in that work for long.
In his thirties, Perrault became an assistant to Jean-Baptiste Colbert, one of the most powerful ministers serving King Louis XIV of France. For twenty years he helped to organise the king's building projects and the arts. He even suggested a maze for the gardens of the Palace of Versailles, filled with fountains showing scenes from Aesop's fables.
Perrault also held an opinion that annoyed many scholars of his time. Most of them believed that the writers of ancient Greece and Rome could never be equalled. Perrault disagreed. He argued that modern writers could be just as good, and he was not afraid to say so in public.
When Colbert died, Perrault lost his position. His wife had died some years earlier, and he now had more time to spend with his children. Perhaps it was during those years, sitting by the fire, that he began to think seriously about the old stories told to children by nurses and servants.
In 1697, when he was almost seventy, a small book appeared called Stories or Tales from Times Past. It contained eight tales, including Little Red Riding Hood and Cinderella, and each one ended with a short rhyming moral. Curiously, the book was published under the name of his teenage son, Pierre. Historians still argue about why.
Perrault did not invent these tales. Versions of them had been passed down by word of mouth for centuries. But he gave them a lively, polished style that delighted readers, and he showed that simple folk stories were worthy of a printed book. In a way, it was the perfect proof of his old argument: a modern storyteller had created something that would outlast almost everything else he wrote.

AnswerB: in Paris in 1628
AnswerC: in Rome in 1628

Wire Across the Red
(A linesman writes home, 1872)
You ask me, Kate, in every letter
why I won't come home this year,
and why a desk in town's not better
than the flies and heat out here.
So here's my answer, plain and true,
by lamplight, short and clear:
the thing we're building's something new,
and that is why I'm here.
First, think how long a letter takes
from here to London town:
two months by ship, for goodness' sake,
with storms to slow it down.
But once this line is joined up north
to cables on the ocean floor,
our words will flash out, back and forth,
in hours, not months, from shore to shore.
At every station, built of stone,
a man will sit all day
and tap the clicks out, on his own,
to send them on their way.
Second, the work is hard but good.
We dig each hole by hand
and stand the poles of sawn hardwood
across the red, flat land.
The summer sun beats like a drum
upon my battered hat,
and flies, a thousand, buzz and hum
and laugh at every swat.
The white ants chewed the timber through
(they think we've brought them lunch!),
so now we're hauling iron, too,
that no white ant can munch.
We haul the wire by bullock dray
and camels, nose to tail,
and string it on, from day to day,
mile after dusty mile.
We've crossed the ranges, red and steep,
and plains as bare as bone;
the stars hang low above our sleep
like lamps we've never known.
And third, I've mates who share my tent,
my damper and my tea,
and when one man is sick or spent,
the rest pitch in, you see.
On Sundays, when the work is still,
we wash our shirts and sing,
and Paddy plays his fiddle till
the gum trees seem to ring.
But since you've asked me, Kate, I'll say
the rest, and tell it true:
the nights are long, and far away
is very far from you.
I keep your letters in my coat
and read them by the fire;
I've learnt by heart the last you wrote.
It travels with the wire.
Each pole we raise, I count as one
more day gone by, and then
I think: when all these poles are done,
I'll see your face again.
So wait for me one season more.
When this long line is done,
a telegram will reach your door:
'Your Dad is coming home.'
QuestionText: What is the poem mainly about?
AnswerA: a daughter's long journey to visit her father in the outback
AnswerB: the trouble caused by white ants in the Australian bush
AnswerC: a father explaining why he is working on the telegraph line
AnswerD: the invention of the telegraph by engineers in England

ComprehensionText:
Time Capsules Made of Ice
Every winter, snow falls on the vast ice sheet that covers Antarctica. In the coldest parts of the continent, that snow almost never melts. Instead, each new layer presses down on the layers beneath it, squeezing them slowly into solid ice. Over hundreds of thousands of years, this process has built ice more than three kilometres thick. To scientists, this ice is far more than frozen water. It is a record of Earth's past, stacked layer upon layer like the pages of a book.
To read this record, scientists drill an ice core. A hollow drill bores down into the ice and brings up a long cylinder, usually about ten centimetres across. The core is cut into sections about a metre long, labelled carefully and kept frozen at all times, both on the ice and on the long journey back to laboratories. A single deep drilling project can take several summers to complete.
What makes ice cores so valuable is what is trapped inside them. As snow turns to ice, tiny bubbles of air are sealed in. These bubbles are samples of the atmosphere as it was when the ice formed. By measuring the gases in them, scientists can find out how much carbon dioxide was in the air thousands of years ago, long before anyone was able to measure it directly. The ice itself also holds clues about past temperatures, while thin bands of ash reveal when distant volcanoes erupted.
The oldest continuous ice core yet drilled, from a site called Dome C, reaches back about 800 000 years. It shows that Earth's climate has swung between long ice ages and warmer periods many times. It also shows that carbon dioxide levels rose and fell along with temperature. Today's carbon dioxide levels are higher than at any point in that entire record.
Scientists are not finished yet. Teams are now searching for ice that is more than a million years old, hoping to understand why the rhythm of the ice ages changed long ago. Finding the right spot is difficult. The ice must be very old, undisturbed and not melted at its base by heat from the rock below.
It may seem strange that some of the most important clues about our climate are hidden in the emptiest place on Earth. Yet in Antarctica, the past has been waiting quietly, frozen in place, for anyone patient enough to dig it up.

AnswerB: about 80 000 years
AnswerC: about 800 000 years

8 India didn't say another word, because at that precise moment, Farmer Austin's prizewinning cow, Bessie, pulled away from her owner's normally strong grip and stampeded through the crowd.

9 "Bessie!"

10 People dove out of the way, sending chairs flying as Bessie zigzagged toward the podium, straight toward India.

11 "Oh no," she breathed.

12 Dad leaped onto the stage and swept her out of the way just as the cow barreled past, knocking over the microphone stand and tearing through the school's specially made banner.

13 "Bessie!" Austin sprinted after his cow, who at that moment crashed into the refreshment stand, splashing juice onto everyone nearby. That's when Austin realized where she was headed.

14 "Watch out, Mrs. O'Donnell!"

16 Austin finally managed to reach her. He offered her hay from his back pocket. "Sorry, everyone. She's normally very calm, but lamingtons drive her bananas."

17 India stared down Main Street from the safety of the podium. Bessie had left quite a trail of destruction: upturned tables and a carpet of squashed cakes and scones.

18 Dad muttered to India, "Your speech needs to be good to top that."

22 "I don't know what it is," Mrs. Rahim said as she tried to catch her breath, "but it seems important. I can feel it."

24 "What does it say?" Dad asked.

25 Everyone gathered closer as India read it aloud, being careful not to miss a single word.

The Light That Didn't Blink
'It's ten to five,' Tess hissed, shaking her brother's shoulder. 'Get up, or you'll miss it.'
Noah pulled the doona over his head. 'Miss what? It's still the middle of the night.'
'The space station. It's passing over at three minutes past five. I told you yesterday.'
She had told him, and he had nodded without listening, the way he did whenever Tess talked about space. She had posters of nebulas above her bed and an app on her phone that showed where the International Space Station was at every moment. Noah thought it was all a bit much.
Still, he followed her out onto the driveway in his slippers. The air was so cold that his breath hung in front of him like smoke. Above the rooftops, the sky was black and crowded with stars, and only a faint grey line showed in the east.
'Where do I look?' he grumbled.
'North-west. Low down, near that gum tree. It'll rise slowly and go almost straight over us.'
Noah stared at the gum tree. Nothing happened. He was about to say so when Tess grabbed his arm.
A point of light had appeared above the branches. At first he thought it was a plane, but it made no sound and it didn't flash red and green. It simply glided, bright and steady, brighter than any star, climbing higher and higher.

ComprehensionText:
Cities Carved from Winter
In many places, winter is a season to be endured. You pull on extra layers, hurry from one warm building to the next and count the weeks until spring. But in some of the coldest cities on Earth, people have decided to do the opposite. Instead of hiding from winter, they throw it a party.
The most dazzling of these may be the Harbin International Ice and Snow Sculpture Festival in north-east China. Each winter, workers saw enormous blocks of ice from the frozen Songhua River and haul them into the city. Teams of builders and artists then stack and carve them into towering castles, bridges and slides. At night, coloured lights are placed inside the ice, and the whole frozen city glows like a box of jewels. Temperatures can fall below minus twenty degrees Celsius, yet huge crowds of visitors arrive every year.
Japan's Sapporo Snow Festival began more modestly. In 1950, a group of local high school students built six snow statues in a city park. Crowds came to look, and the idea snowballed. Today the festival features hundreds of sculptures, some as big as buildings, and draws visitors from around the world each February.
In Canada, the Quebec Winter Carnival is famous for its mascot, Bonhomme, a cheerful snowman in a red cap and a colourful sash. Visitors can watch canoe races across the icy St Lawrence River, where teams paddle, push and drag their boats over floating chunks of ice.
Why would anyone celebrate the cold? For one thing, these festivals turn a difficult season into something to look forward to. They bring neighbours outside when they might otherwise stay indoors for months. They also attract tourists, which helps local businesses during a quiet time of year.
Perhaps most importantly, they show something about human imagination. Ice and snow cannot be kept. Every sculpture, however grand, will crack, slump and melt away when spring arrives. The builders know this before they begin. They carve anyway, for the joy of making something beautiful that lasts only a few weeks.

AnswerB: the frozen Songhua River
AnswerC: a city park in Sapporo

Dancing Dragons

1 In fairy tales, dragons are ferocious creatures. However, in Chinese culture, dragons are not fire-breathing enemies. They are kind creatures that drive away bad luck and bring good fortune. Every year at the Spring Festival, also known as Chinese New Year, the dragons are dancers!

2 In ancient China, people performed the dragon dance to bring more rain. Now, the dance is performed to ensure a good new year. During the Spring Festival, there is a parade that features the dragon dance. This dance is performed by an enormous dragon that is held up by several strong dancers using poles.

3 A dragon is created with joints that allow it to bend easily. The body of the dragon is made of thin bamboo strips. They are woven into cylinders, or large tubes. Then, the dragon is covered in a giant cloth. It is decorated with scales. Most dragons are red. Red symbolizes happiness in Chinese culture. Dragons can be hundreds of feet long!

4 During the parade, one person holds a stick with a large ball that holds the dragon's head. They lead the dragon through the city's streets. Behind the head, there are people holding poles to support sections of the dragon. The people wear clothing the same color as the dragon. This makes their legs look like the legs of the dragon. As the head dips and dives, so does the dragon. It looks like the dragon is dancing! People along the parade route watch and cheer as the dragon weaves back and forth. Its long body ripples like a ribbon.

5 There is also a fire dragon that dances at night. Inside fire dragons are candles or lamps. The skin of the dragon is thin cloth or paper. The light can be seen through the skin. When this dragon dances at night, it looks like it is filled with fire.

6 For centuries, Chinese communities across the globe have gathered in this way to celebrate spring. With the dragon's help, they hope to bring happiness in the year ahead.

ComprehensionText:
Four-Winged Hunters
If you have ever sat beside a pond on a summer afternoon, you have probably seen a dragonfly zipping over the water like a tiny jet. It is easy to admire their shimmering wings and bright colours. But do not be fooled by their beauty. Dragonflies are among the most successful hunters in the animal kingdom.
Ancient flyers
Dragonflies have been around for an astonishingly long time. Their ancestors were flying through forests about 300 million years ago, long before the first dinosaurs appeared. Some of those early relatives were giants, with wings that stretched about 70 centimetres from tip to tip. Scientists think the air at that time held more oxygen than it does today, which may have helped insects grow so large.
Masters of the air
A dragonfly has four wings, and each one is powered by its own set of muscles, so it can move each wing separately. As a result, a dragonfly can hover, fly backwards and change direction in an instant.
Its eyes are just as impressive. Each huge compound eye is made up of thousands of tiny lenses, and together the two eyes wrap almost all the way around its head. A dragonfly can see in nearly every direction at once, tracking a small fly as it darts through the air.
Put these skills together and you have a remarkable predator. In some studies, dragonflies caught their prey in more than nine out of every ten attempts. Lions, by comparison, succeed only about a quarter of the time.
A secret life underwater
Most people never see the longest part of a dragonfly's life. Dragonflies lay their eggs in or near water, and the young, called nymphs, live beneath the surface for months or even years. A nymph is a fierce hunter too. It has a hinged lower lip that shoots forward in a fraction of a second to grab tadpoles, small fish and insect larvae.
When it is fully grown, the nymph climbs up a reed, splits its skin and slowly pulls out its new body and crumpled wings. Within hours, a new adult takes to the sky.
So the next time a dragonfly flashes past you, take a moment to watch. You are looking at one of nature's most ancient and skilful hunters, and I think that is something worth stopping for.

AnswerD: They lay their eggs in or near the water.

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
Ivar and the flying fish

Ivar's new method of fishing had exceeded all expectations. Never in the history of their small Viking community had such an enormous number of fish been caught in less than one hour, and by a 12-year-old boy—albeit an intellectually gifted one. Ivar calculated his catch to be the finest on record. This 'finest on record' catch, however, presented a slight problem: how to preserve 756 herrings really quickly.

Ivar immediately applied his considerable intellect to solving the problem.

He went to his favourite thinking place, overlooking the fjord. The wind was brisk and icy. It whistled up the fjord; it always did as winter attempted to reassert its authority over spring. The icy water of the fjord below rippled in response to the tugging winds just as an idea tugged at Ivar's thoughts. He grabbed a piece of bone and sketched a rough diagram in the dirt. His new idea was inspired by a wooden propeller he had designed for the family boat some years earlier; it had long since been used as firewood. Ivar considered that the wind might do the work of rotating the propeller blades. His fish would be tied to the blades and, in the blustery conditions of early spring, would be very efficiently wind dried!

Ivar was buzzing! He thrived on the inspiration-to-implementation of the design process. His precious elk horn collection would provide the material for the blades and a recently felled tree would make a sturdy vertical post. Ivar was busy!

Hours later, as dusk fell and the residents prepared their evening meals, a strange thudding noise was heard on nearly every mud roof in the village. Those villagers who had timber roofs described the sound as closer to a 'strange clattering noise'. Either way, there was something peculiar happening that evening.

High above the village, in his beloved (but currently very windy) thinking place, Ivar had a different problem. He was struggling to keep the fish tied to the blades of his turbine-type machine. The device worked too well—currently it was rotating at 15 revolutions per minute even with 150 or so medium-sized fish strapped on—and threatened to lift off its hillside perch. He had lost at least 60 fish in the last few minutes, and who knew where they had landed?
QuestionText: When the writer comments about winter's attempt 'to reassert its authority over spring', she means that
AnswerA: the weather conditions were unusual for spring.
AnswerB: winter is a much harsher season than spring.
AnswerC: the weather in early spring can still be cold.
AnswerD: spring is a much shorter season than winter.

Thirty Languages in Cooma
Anna's first word of English was 'snow', and she learned it the week her family arrived in Cooma in the winter of 1952.
Her father had come from Norway six months earlier to work on the Snowy Mountains Scheme, the enormous project to build dams, tunnels and power stations in the mountains of New South Wales. Now Anna, her mother and her baby brother had followed him across the world. From the bus window, Cooma looked small and wind-swept, with rows of new houses and muddy streets. But on the main street, Anna heard more languages in five minutes than she had heard in her whole life: Italian, German, Polish, Greek, Dutch and others she couldn't name.
'Men from more than thirty countries,' her father told her. 'All here to bring water and electricity to Australia.'
School was the hardest part. On her first morning, the teacher, Mrs Hartley, wrote 'Welcome Anna' on the blackboard and pointed to a seat next to a girl with dark plaits. The girl was called Lucia, and she was from Italy. She knew only a few more English words than Anna, but she smiled and pushed half of her pencils across the desk.
For weeks the two girls spoke in a mixture of English, pointing and drawings. Lucia taught Anna 'playground' and 'lunch'. Anna taught Lucia how to make a snow angel. When Mrs Hartley asked the class to draw where their fathers worked, the girls discovered that their fathers were digging the same tunnel, one from each end.
In the evenings, Anna's father came home grey with rock dust, so tired he sometimes fell asleep at the table. Anna's mother worried, but her father always said the same thing: 'One day you will switch on a light, and some of that power will come from our mountain.'
By spring, Anna could read simple books in English. She still spoke Norwegian at home, but at school she sometimes forgot which language she was using until she saw Lucia laughing.
Years later, when the tunnel was finished, the two families stood together at the opening ceremony. Anna and Lucia, now taller than their mothers, held hands as the water rushed through the mountain their fathers had joined.

Tree Keeper
Ares Dome, Mars. Sol 412 (that's a Tuesday, for anyone reading this on Earth)
Dear Diary,
Today started as the most boring day in the history of Mars. The dust storm has been blowing for nine sols, so outdoor walks are cancelled, the windows are brown, and the only thing on the learning screen was a lesson about air filters. AIR FILTERS. I live in a dome where the air is filtered every second of every day. I think I know about air filters.
Then, after lunch, Commander Osei made an announcement. The cargo lander that touched down before the storm had brought something special, and everyone was to meet in the Green Bay at fifteen hundred hours.
The Green Bay is where we grow lettuce, tomatoes and beans under pink lights. It always smells damp and a bit like socks. Today it was packed. Right in the middle, in a big pot, stood a tree.
Okay, it was not a big tree. It was about as tall as me, with a thin grey trunk and maybe forty leaves. The label said Eucalyptus, which Dad says is from Australia, where he grew up. But it was a TREE, Diary. A real one, not a picture or a hologram.
Here's the strange part. The adults who were born on Earth went very quiet. Mrs Petrova put her hand over her mouth. Dad crouched down, crushed a leaf between his fingers and breathed in, and his eyes went shiny. He said it smelt like a summer holiday he had when he was nine.
When it was my turn, I touched the trunk. It was smooth in some places and peeling in others, as if it were taking off an old jacket. I crushed a leaf too. It smelt sharp and clean, like medicine, but alive. It didn't remind me of anything, because I don't have any summer holidays on Earth to remember. Still, my chest felt tight, in a good way.
The botanists say that if the tree survives, its seeds could one day grow a whole grove inside the new dome. I asked if I could help look after it. Dr Ahmed said yes, on Thursdays.
So now I have a job. Tree Keeper, Ares Dome. The storm is still blowing, but I don't mind so much any more.
Leo

AnswerB: calm and thoughtful
AnswerC: proud and boastful

Walk through our town mall on a Saturday morning and what do you hear? The beep of a pedestrian crossing, the rumble of delivery trucks and perhaps a crying toddler. What you will not hear is music. Since the council introduced strict new rules last year, buskers have almost vanished from our streets. I believe these rules should be relaxed, and street performers welcomed back.
Under the current rules, buskers must buy a permit costing one hundred dollars, perform only in two small marked squares beside the car park and finish by eleven o'clock in the morning. For a teenager hoping to earn a little pocket money with a guitar, that is a steep price for a spot that hardly anyone walks past.
Street music brings life to a town. A violinist playing outside the bakery makes people slow down, smile and linger. When shoppers linger, they spend. Shop owners in many other towns have found that a lively street draws more customers, not fewer. Music is an invitation; silence is a shrug.
Busking also gives young performers a stage. Not every talented musician can book a concert hall. Some of Australia's best-known performers began by playing on footpaths, learning to win over people who had not come to hear them. That is a tough audience, and it builds skill and confidence quickly.
Finally, buskers make music free for everyone. A concert ticket can cost more than many families can afford. On the street, a child can stop and watch a juggling drummer for as long as they like, and pay nothing more than a clap.
Of course, the council has reasons for its rules. Some shopkeepers complained about performers who were too loud or who played the same three songs all day. These concerns are fair. But the answer is not to drive buskers away; it is to set sensible limits. A cheap permit, a volume limit and a rule that performers move spots every two hours would solve most problems without silencing anyone.
Our mall was built for people, and people have always gathered around music. Let's change the rules, unpack the guitar cases and let the mall sing again.

The Downwind family, members of the Ojibwe tribe in Minnesota, travel to ceremonial gatherings called powwows. from Powwow Summer by Marcie Rendon Karla, a cousin of the Downwind children, wears a beautiful jingle dress.

1 All around the world, people have special outfits to wear at ceremonies. Easter outfits, prom dresses, and tuxedos are worn for different occasions. At powwows, the Downwind women wear the jingle dress or the fancy-shawl-dance outfit.

2 Sharyl is a jingle-dress dancer. On her dress are hundreds of metal cones, or jingles. It can take a long time to hand-roll these jingles into the cone shape. To be a jingle-dress dancer requires special patience.

3 The idea for the jingle dress was dreamt by an Ojibwe man many years ago. This is the story Sharyl tells her daughters:

4 A long time ago, there was a man who loved his daughter very much. His daughter became very sick, close to death. The father was very worried about her and prayed for her to be well. In the dream, the father also heard the songs that were to be sung for the women as they danced wearing the jingle dress. In his dream, he saw the women dancing. When he awoke from his dream, he shared his vision with his wife. Together, they worked to make the jingle dress for their daughter. The father taught the songs to the singers of the village. When all this was done and the daughter wore the dress and danced, she became well.

5 From this girl's family, the jingle dress spread to many other tribes. In the Downwind family, Sasina, Star, and Danielle are jingle-dress dancers. Shian, Katie, Ronee, Valentina, and Keisha are fancy-shawl dancers. The outfit for this dance consists of a knee-length dress, matching leggings, moccasins, and a fancy shawl with fringe or ribbon that floats with the dancer's elegant movements and fancy dance steps. It is thought that shawl dancing developed as shawls replaced the blankets and animal robes worn by young women years ago.

2 In ancient China, people performed the dragon dance to bring more rain. Now, the dance is performed to ensure a good new year. During the Spring Festival, there is a parade that features the dragon dance. This dance is performed by an enormous dragon that is held up by several strong dancers using poles.

3 A dragon is created with joints that allow it to bend easily. The body of the dragon is made of thin bamboo strips. They are woven into cylinders, or large tubes. Then, the dragon is covered in a giant cloth. It is decorated with scales. Most dragons are red. Red symbolizes happiness in Chinese culture. Dragons can be hundreds of feet long!

As the head dips and dives, so does the dragon. It looks like the dragon is dancing! People along the parade route watch and cheer as the dragon weaves back and forth. Its long body ripples like a ribbon.

5 There is also a fire dragon that dances at night. Inside fire dragons are candles or lamps. The skin of the dragon is thin cloth or paper. The light can be seen through the skin. When this dragon dances at night, it looks like it is filled with fire.

6 For centuries, Chinese communities across the globe have gathered in this way to celebrate spring. With the dragon's help, they hope to bring happiness in the year ahead.

The year is 1150 BC. The location is a meadow not far from Stonehenge in Britain.

'Are we all present?' boomed Drystan, the 'leader' of our little band, while adjusting his lately acquired deerskin cloak which he wore as his symbol of leadership.

Eleven voices murmured agreement and one asked, 'Is this a birthday party?'

'No laughter in the stone circle' Drystan tried to boom again while undoing the bone toggle of his cloak which was threatening to constrict his breathing.

'The purpose of our meeting today is to discuss design ideas for a small shelter so we can have our meetings in all weather conditions, Drystan informed us.

'We could use a few animal skins stretched over a timber frame,' I suggested.

'That's a dumb idea, Anyou, Drystan intoned.

Clearly, praise and encouragement were aspects of leadership that Drystan needed to develop further.

'We will build our shelter using stone,' stated Drystan.

'Yes, Drystan. Of course, Drystan,' we all chimed.

All day we collected stones, piling, wedging and balancing them until we had a shelter that looked like it had been designed by a landslide. Still, it seemed to please Drystan and that's all that mattered really. The last job of the day involved rolling an extra large log near the entrance to the shelter. Drystan would use this as his podium when he was directing his horde of followers.

Dutifully we pushed the designated log in the approximate direction of the shelter. The remaining events are listed in our (secret) meeting records as follows:

1. After a bit of a push, the log gathered speed as a result of a slight incline.
2. The log took off on its own accord and proceeded (quickly) in a northerly direction towards Stonehenge.
3. The log came to rest against a stone pillar at the entrance and the pillar was dislodged.
4. Large stones fell like dominoes around the circle that was Stonehenge.
5. In unspoken agreement we all left the scene immediately. Drystan had a head start on all of us.

A few months later I overheard a conversation among the village elders as to the cause of the Stonehenge catastrophe. One voice was louder than the rest: 'An unusual alignment of stars in combination with a rainbow and an easterly wind!' I recognised it as the voice of Drystan's father. The other elders nodded their agreement. Drystan must have inherited his father's leadership skills, I concluded, because they both have strong voices.
QuestionText: According to Anyou, why was Drystan the leader?
AnswerB: He had the cleverest ideas.
AnswerC: He had a father whom the children feared.
AnswerD: He had been given a symbol of leadership.

During those barren winter months, with windows overlooking longdead gardens, leafless trees, and lawns that seem to have an ashy look about them, nothing soothes the jangled nerves more than the vibrant green of plants surrounding the living spaces of one's home. People browse through garden stores just to get a whiff of chlorophyll and to choose a plant or two to bring spring back into their winter-gray lives.

Now there is even more of a need for "the green," in light of recent articles warning us of the hazards of chemicals that we, ourselves, introduce into our homes. Each time we bring clothes home from the cleaners, we release those chemicals into the closed-in air of our dwellings. Every cleanser releases its own assortment of fumes. Some of the chemicals are formaldehyde, chlorine, benzene, styrene, etc. Read the labels on many home products, the ingredients aren't even listed! During the winter, when those same windows are shut tight, we breathe in these chemicals—causing symptoms much like allergies. In fact, most people probably dismiss the effects of these chemicals simply as a flare up of some allergy or other. The truth is that we are experiencing a syndrome that is called Multiple Chemical Sensitivity. Now, what has this got to do with green plants? Everything healthy! Research has been conducted with two types of plants that have actually removed much of these harmful chemicals from the air.

The two plants that seem to be the best bet for ridding one's home of such chemicals are ferns and palms. These plants release moisture as part of photosynthesis and, as they do, pull chemicals from the air into their leaves. Even NASA has conducted some greenhouse experiments for long-term space exploration. Within hours, their plants [palms] had removed almost all traces of formaldehyde in the room. Both species of plants are ancient, dating back more than a hundred million years. Another trait they share is that they both live long lives, 100 years or more. This we expect from trees, but ferns and palms are plants; plants that can grow to 65 feet in the proper setting! Even their individual leaves live for one to two years [ferns] and one to nine years [palms]. Perhaps it is their primal qualities that have contributed to their ability to purify their environment.
QuestionText: The passage infers a relationship between the antiquity of ferns and palms and their ability to
AnswerB: purify the air.
AnswerC: grow leaves that live long.

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
Read this story. Then answer questions 29 through 35.

In a faraway kingdom called Tellus, Aleks signs up for the army. Then he finds out what a dishonest and brutal place it is.

Excerpt from The Almost King by Lucy Saxon

1 Slinging his light saddlebag over his shoulders and swallowing his cry of pain at the movement, he pulled his hat low over his forehead and made for the door. He needed his enlistment forms from Shulga's office; if he could find and destroy them, the army would have no record of him enlisting. Even if he did get caught after escaping—provided he escaped in the first place—there would be no proof that he was a cadet.^1 Then all he had to do was reach the stables and get Quicksilver before anyone on the dinner shift noticed what he was doing. After that . . . he would find a way out. There had to be one somewhere. . . .

2 There were no guards at the door; the barracks^2 was down to a skeleton guard for the dinner shift. Aleks silently retraced his steps from earlier in the day, making his way towards Antova's office. His eyes raced over every door's nameplate, frowning when none of them was the office he was looking for. He was incredibly short on time; he had to be on Quicksilver and heading for freedom before dinner ended.

3 Finally, he saw it. Lt. Shulga was embossed on a nameplate three doors down from Antova's. Luckily, the door was unlocked and the room empty; Shulga had obviously gone straight from the time-out room to dinner. The office was decorated in the same way as Antova's, in blue and dark brown, with a large map of Tellus on the wall instead of the royal crest the commander displayed. Darting across to a metal filing cabinet that took up most of one wall, Aleks wrenched open a drawer at random, ignoring the searing ache in his arms. Again, unlocked. Clearly Shulga was too cocky to think anyone would dare snoop around his office.

4 The drawer was full of neatly filed enlistment forms in alphabetical order; F–J. Aleks's form would come under V. Shutting the drawer, he reached for the next one, perplexed to find it containing M–P. The drawer after that didn't contain enlistment forms at all, but instead held a large stack of account books. Shulga didn't seem to have any sort of system whatsoever; how did he ever find anything he needed?

Page 2 Session 2

5 Growling in frustration, Aleks began to open multiple drawers at a time, rifling through stacks of papers and leather-bound books, his desperation growing with every unsuccessful attempt. Digging through a drawer of miscellaneous files and books closest to the desk, his fingers scrabbled at the bottom of the drawer and it tilted a fraction, sending three stacked files slumping against a small metal box. 'What the . . .' He trailed off, pressing harder on the base of the drawer, watching it dip under his fingers. The drawer had a false bottom!

6 Aleks glanced at the clock; he knew he shouldn't, but he'd always been the curious type. Emptying the drawer, he dug his nails under one side of the fake bottom, prising it up. The secret compartment was fairly narrow, containing only a thin file of papers and a battered leather journal. It was the journal that caught Aleks's eye, for it had the Anglyan crest embossed in one corner of the cover. What on Tellus was Shulga doing with an Anglyan journal? . . .

7 A door slamming somewhere in the building startled him out of his horrified trance, and a quick look at the clock nearly gave Aleks a heart attack. He barely had ten minutes until the end of dinner!

8 Stuffing the journal in an inner pocket of his coat, he hastily replaced the drawer's false bottom and contents, shutting it as quietly as he could. Tugging on the two drawers he had yet to check, he swore under his breath. Neither of them contained a V section, and Aleks felt dread creep over him at the realization that his file was likely elsewhere. He didn't have the time to search any other rooms. Out of options, he straightened up, shoving all the cabinet drawers shut and sprinting for the door.

9 A quick glance through the glass panel showed the corridor to be empty, so Aleks slipped from the room.

10 Bursting through the door of the building, he turned for the stables, slowing his pace once he hit the cobblestone path, just in case anyone happened to look his way. There was nothing more suspicious than a lone cadet running.

11 While there was supposed to be at least one stablehand in the building at all times, Aleks couldn't see a single soul in the stables. Perfect. Hurrying to the tack^3 room, he easily found Quicksilver's saddle and bridle, though carrying the heavy items in his current state nearly sent him crumpling to the floor. Still, he forced himself to ignore the pain, hefting the tack across the room towards Quicksilver's stall. Session 2 Page 3

12 The horse whinnied when he saw the tack, knowing what it meant. Aleks shushed him, slinging the saddle on the door and slipping inside, easing the bridle on to the horse's head. Tossing the saddle on Quicksilver's back, he fastened it tightly and slung the saddlebag over the horse's rear, buckling it swiftly. He grabbed the reins, running to press Quicksilver's nose to his chest for a brief moment. 'We need to be quiet, boy. No getting excited.' ____ cadet: new member of the armed services 1 barracks: place where soldiers sleep 2 tack: stable gear such as saddles and bridles 3
QuestionText: How does Aleks's attitude change in paragraph 5?
AnswerA: It shifts from exhausted to curious.
AnswerB: It shifts from panicked to confident.
AnswerC: It shifts from distracted to focused.
AnswerD: It shifts from annoyed to surprised.

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
The Brown Lump on the Window
The brown lump had been stuck to the classroom window frame since the end of autumn. It was about the size of a walnut, papery and ridged, and most of Class 7B assumed it was an old wasp nest or a blob of dried glue. Only Mr Okafor seemed interested in it. He had stuck a strip of masking tape beside it with a single word written in marker: WAIT.
'It's an ootheca,' he told Noor when she finally asked in July. 'A praying mantis egg case. The mother made it from a foam that hardened, and there could be a hundred eggs inside. They'll hatch when the weather warms up.'
Noor didn't believe him, but she began checking it every morning anyway.
Weeks passed. Nothing happened. The lump just sat there, brown and boring, while winter rain streamed down the glass. Some of the boys drew two columns on the whiteboard, ALIVE and DEAD, and the class voted. Noor wrote her name under ALIVE, mostly because nobody else had.
Then, on a warm Tuesday in October, she walked into the classroom early and stopped dead.
The window was moving.
Tiny pale shapes were wriggling out from the bottom of the ootheca, dangling on fine silky threads like acrobats on ropes. Each one was no bigger than a grain of rice. As she watched, they shook themselves loose and began to climb, their long front legs folded in front of their faces as though they were already praying. Within minutes there were dozens of them, scattered across the glass like spilled punctuation.
'Mr Okafor!' she called, not taking her eyes off the window.
He came in with his coffee, saw the window and smiled so widely that he forgot to drink it.
By the time the bell rang, the whole class was crowded around, whispering as if the hatchlings might hear them. Mr Okafor explained that the babies were called nymphs and looked like tiny adults, with no caterpillar stage, and that they would shed their skins several times as they grew. Then he said they would need to carry the nymphs out to the school garden straight away.
'Why can't we keep them?' asked Jacob, whose name was under DEAD.
'Because they'll eat each other,' said Mr Okafor.
There was a horrified silence.
'Mantises eat whatever is small enough to catch,' he said, 'and right now the smallest things around are their brothers and sisters. Out in the garden they'll spread out and find aphids and tiny flies. In here, crowded together, they'd soon start on each other.'
So 7B spent the first lesson of the day kneeling in the garden, gently tipping nymphs off pieces of card onto leaves. And the masking tape stayed on the window frame until the end of the year, still saying WAIT.
QuestionText: What word did Mr Okafor write on the masking tape?
AnswerB: ALIVE
AnswerC: OOTHECA

Nine Logs and an Ocean
In April 1947, six men pushed off from the coast of Peru on a raft that many experts were sure would sink. It had no engine and no modern hull, just nine logs of balsa wood lashed together with rope, a small bamboo cabin and a square sail. Its name was Kon-Tiki, and its leader was a Norwegian explorer named Thor Heyerdahl.
Heyerdahl had a bold idea. He believed that people from South America might have sailed west across the Pacific long ago and settled the islands of Polynesia. Most scientists disagreed. They argued that ancient South Americans had no boats capable of such a journey. Heyerdahl decided there was only one way to answer them: build a raft from materials those people could have used, and sail it himself.
Before they left, the doubters were loud. Balsa, they warned, would soak up water and become too heavy to float. The ropes would rub through. The crew would be lucky to last a fortnight.
The ocean had other plans. Carried by the trade winds and a strong current, the raft drifted steadily westward. The logs did absorb some water, but they stayed afloat. The ropes sank into the soft balsa instead of fraying against it. The men fished, collected rainwater and woke most mornings to find flying fish that had landed on the deck overnight. One day a whale shark, the largest fish in the sea, circled the raft, its spotted back sliding beneath the logs while the crew watched nervously.
After 101 days and nearly 7,000 kilometres, the voyage ended with a crash. Waves drove the raft onto a coral reef near the island of Raroia, and the crew scrambled through the surf to the shore. Battered but unhurt, they had crossed a large part of the Pacific Ocean.
Heyerdahl's book about the expedition was translated into dozens of languages, and a film of the journey won an Academy Award. Around the world, readers were thrilled by the story of a few determined people taking on the ocean with an ancient design.
Yet the voyage did not settle the scientific question. It proved that such a trip was possible, not that it had actually happened. Later studies of language, objects and DNA suggest that Polynesians came mainly from the west, from islands closer to Asia, although some evidence hints at contact with South Americans many centuries ago.
Even so, Kon-Tiki showed something valuable. Sometimes the best way to test an idea is to step off the shore and try it.

Some Assembly Required
The box said SOME ASSEMBLY REQUIRED in cheerful red letters. Dad said it the same way, rubbing his hands together.
“Forty minutes, tops,” he announced confidently, slicing open the cardboard with a butter knife because he couldn't find the scissors.
I'm Lachie, I'm twelve, and I have learnt that when Dad says forty minutes, you should pack a lunch.
Inside the box were six long panels, a heap of screws, a tiny metal tool shaped like an L, and a booklet of instructions with no words at all, just drawings of a smiling cartoon man. Dad flicked through it once and tossed it onto the couch.
“Instructions are for people who don't understand furniture,” he said.
The first hour went quite well. The sides went on. The top went on. The back panel went on upside down, came off, and went on again the right way up, but we agreed not to mention that to Mum.
Then Dad found a little plastic bag marked C. Inside were sixteen small wooden pegs, each about the size of a fat matchstick.
“Spares,” he said, dropping the bag into the box with the cardboard. “They always give you spares.”
I wasn't so sure. Running my finger along the inside of the bookcase, I could feel rows of small round holes beneath where each shelf would sit. I picked up the booklet. On page six, the smiling cartoon man was pushing tiny pegs into tiny holes. He looked very pleased with himself.
“Dad –”
“Not now, mate. Pass me the shelves.”
He slid the four shelves into place. They balanced there, resting on almost nothing, looking proud and level. Dad stood back, spread his arms wide and declared it a masterpiece. Two hours and fifty minutes, but who was counting? (Me. I was counting.)
Mum came in to admire it. Dad, beaming, began loading my entire collection of encyclopaedias onto the top shelf.
“Dad,” I said again. “Page six.”
“Lachie, trust me.”
Creak.
We all looked at the top shelf.
Creeeeak.
Mum quietly stepped back. I quietly stepped back. Dad, still holding the last encyclopaedia, did not.
CRASH.
The top shelf dropped onto the second, which dropped onto the third, which dropped onto the fourth, and the whole lot ended in a heap of books and boards at the bottom, like a very tidy avalanche.
For a long moment, nobody spoke. Then Mum reached into the cardboard box, pulled out the little bag marked C and held it up to the light.
Dad looked at the bag. He looked at the booklet on the couch. He looked at me.
“Right,” he said slowly. “Page six, you said?”

AnswerD: Dad's jobs usually take much longer than he says

ComprehensionText:
The Long Way Round Wattle Street
Every September, Nell's walk to school became a battle. Halfway down Wattle Street, a magpie would launch from the old gum outside number fourteen, and Nell would hear the whoosh of wings a split second before a beak clacked beside her ear.
For two weeks she tried everything. She wore her bike helmet with cable ties poking out like the spines of an echidna. She waved a stick above her head. She sprinted. Nothing worked. Her friends laughed at the video someone took of her running. If anything, the magpie grew bolder, and Nell began to dread the sound of her front door closing behind her.
One afternoon, red-faced and furious, she stormed past number fourteen just as old Mr Kostas was watering his roses.
"He got you again?" he asked.
"He's a monster," Nell said. "Someone should cut that tree down."
Mr Kostas turned off the hose. "Come and look," he said, pointing up into the gum. High in a fork, Nell could just make out a messy bowl of sticks and the tip of a black-and-white tail.
"His mate is sitting on eggs," Mr Kostas said quietly. "He's not a monster. He's a father. Every person who walks under that tree looks to him like something that might eat his chicks. The stick, the running, the shouting - to him, that just proves he's right."
"So what am I supposed to do?"
"Go around. Six weeks, maybe less, and the babies will be flying."
The detour added ten minutes and one extra hill to Nell's walk. The first morning she grumbled the whole way. By the second week, she had noticed things she'd never seen before: a blue-tongue lizard sunning itself on a letterbox, a lemon tree heavy with fruit, a kelpie that wagged at her through a fence. She started leaving home a little earlier, just so she could stop and look. Some mornings she waved to the kelpie's owner, an old woman in a straw hat, who soon began waving back.
In late October, Mr Kostas waved her over. On his lawn, a fluffy grey bird with a stubby tail was squawking for food, and the magpie was stuffing a beetle down its throat.
Nell kept very still. The magpie looked at her, head tilted, eyes bright, quite unbothered. Then it went back to its work.
The next morning, Nell walked down Wattle Street for the first time in six weeks. As she reached number fourteen, she heard the familiar rush of wings and froze. But the magpie only landed on the fence beside her, threw back its head and poured out a long, warbling song.
Nell laughed. Then, to her own surprise, she turned at the corner and took the long way anyway.

AnswerA: a hat with an echidna's spines
AnswerB: her bike helmet with cable ties
AnswerC: a raincoat with the hood pulled up
AnswerD: her school hat with a stick on top

Building and Trimming a Paper Glider
A paper glider is more than a toy. Every time it floats across a room, it relies on the same four forces that keep a passenger jet in the air. This report explains those forces and then shows you how to build and test a glider of your own.
The four forces
Any aircraft in flight is affected by four forces. Weight is the pull of gravity, dragging the aircraft down. Lift is the upward push created as air flows over and under the wings. Thrust moves the aircraft forward, and drag is the resistance of the air pushing back against it. A jet's engines provide thrust, but a glider has no engine. Its only thrust comes from your throw. After that, it trades height for distance, sliding gently downwards through the air.
Making the glider
You will need a sheet of A4 paper and a paper clip.
1. Fold the paper in half lengthways, crease it firmly, and open it out again.
2. Fold the two top corners in to meet the centre crease, forming a point.
3. Fold the new slanted edges in to the centre crease again, making the point narrower.
4. Fold the whole plane in half along the centre crease, with the folds on the outside.
5. Fold each side down to make the wings, so that the top edge of each wing lines up with the bottom of the body.
6. Open the wings so that they form a slight V shape when viewed from the front.
Testing and trimming
Find a large indoor space, so that wind will not affect your results. Hold the glider under the wings and launch it gently forward and level. Do not throw it hard; a glider flies best at a smooth, steady speed.
Watch carefully how it flies. Pilots and engineers call the small adjustments that follow 'trimming'.
If the glider climbs steeply, slows, then drops suddenly, it is stalling. Its nose is pointing too high, so the wings can no longer produce enough lift. Slide a paper clip onto the nose. The extra weight at the front will help keep the nose down.
If the glider dives straight into the floor, its nose is pointing too low. Bend the back edges of both wings up very slightly, by about two millimetres. Air hitting these raised edges will push the tail down and lift the nose.
If the glider turns sharply to one side, check that both wings are the same shape. Small differences can make a big difference.
Change only one thing at a time, and test it several times before making another change. That way, you will know exactly which adjustment made the difference. Real aircraft designers work in much the same way: testing, adjusting and testing again. Very few planes, paper or otherwise, fly perfectly on the first try.

AnswerB: the air under the wings
AnswerC: the paper clip on the nose

(1) The worst and longest economic crisis in the modern industrial world, the Great Depression in the United States had devastating consequences for American society. At its lowest depth (1932–33), more than 16 million people were unemployed, more than 5,000 banks had closed, and over 85,000 businesses had failed. Millions of Americans lost their jobs, their savings, and even their homes. The homeless built shacks for temporary shelter—these emerging shantytowns were nicknamed Hoovervilles; a bitter homage to President Herbert Hoover, who refused to give government assistance to the jobless. The effects of the Depression—severe unemployment rates and a sharp drop in the production and sales of goods—could also be felt abroad, where many European nations still struggled to recover from World War I.

(2) Although the stock market crash of 1929 marked the onset of the depression, it was not the cause of it: Deep, underlying fissures already existed in the economy of the Roaring Twenties. For example, the tariff and war-debt policies after World War I contributed to the instability of the banking system. American banks made loans to European countries following World War I. However, the United States kept high tariffs on goods imported from other nations. These policies worked against one another. If other countries could not sell goods in the United States, they could not make enough money to pay back their loans or to buy American goods. (3) And while the United States seemed to be enjoying a prosperous period in the 1920s, the wealth was not evenly distributed. Businesses made gains in productivity, but only one segment of the population—the wealthy—reaped large profits. Workers received only a small share of the wealth they helped produce. At the same time, Americans spent more than they earned. Advertising encouraged Americans to buy cars, radios, and household appliances instead of saving or purchasing only what they could afford. Easy credit policies allowed consumers to borrow money and accumulate debt. Investors also wildly speculated on the stock market, often borrowing money on credit to buy shares of a company. Stocks increased beyond their worth, but investors were willing to pay inflated prices because they believed stocks would continue to rise. This bubble burst in the fall of 1929, when investors lost confidence that stock prices would keep rising. As investors sold off stocks, the market spiraled downward. The stock market crash affected the economy in the same way that a stressful event can affect the human body, lowering its resistance to infection.

(4) The ensuing depression led to the election of President Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1932. These measures, called the New Deal, included the Agricultural Adjustment Act, which paid farmers to slow their production in order to stabilize food prices; the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, which insured bank deposits if banks failed; and the Securities and Exchange Commission, which regulated the stock market. In the following passage, the narrator reflects upon his early days in Australia. I discovered that soap operas were excellent learning aids: their plots universal and repetitive, the histrionic acting transpicuous^1; I could concentrate on the colloquial dialogues. I watched the cast of Sons and Daughters squabble and The Young Doctors flirt with the nubile nurses. I sat in front of the TV and repeated the dialogue line by line. I copied the rhythm, the idioms and the tone. I discovered that to learn to speak is to learn to listen.

I couldn't formulate sentences quickly enough to converse at normal speed, so I took to planning for a conversation like for a game of chess; the first 'hello' was the opening gambit. I anticipated all the possible responses from my opponent and devised my replies accordingly. Preparing such a script gave me the semblance of a spontaneous speaker in common situations like asking for directions or ordering fast food. But I was still utterly useless when talking to girls, who always came up with startling lines that reduced me to a stammering idiot. When I did finally think of a witty response, it was usually hours after they had left.

No English teacher in Hong Kong had ever mentioned the prosodic characteristics of the language. It has its own distinctive pitch, melody, tempo and tones. Even meaningful noises, like a grunt for admiration or contempt, are all different in English and Chinese.

Curiously, dozing in a busy shopping mall helped me to tune in to this. In the nevernever land between wakefulness and sleep, vowels and consonants receded while the musical quality of English became prominent; its intonations tintinnabulated like glass bells, its distinct rhythm became a drumbeat I could clap to. My relationship with English became a lot friendlier once I started to learn not just grammar and vocabulary, but also to listen to its music.

The Spare Key
Aunt Fen's van smelt of machine oil and peppermints. Rows of tiny drawers lined the back, each labelled in her neat capitals: BLANKS, SPRINGS, PINS, CYLINDERS, and one marked simply ODDS. On the first day of the school holidays, Tilly climbed into the passenger seat with a notebook and a promise to touch nothing without asking.
'Being a locksmith is only half about locks,' Aunt Fen said as they pulled away from the kerb. 'The other half is people. Nobody calls me on their best day.'
The morning's jobs were quick. A café owner had snapped a key in the back door, and Aunt Fen slid two slender tools into the lock and drew out the broken half as neatly as a splinter. Then she cut a new key on the grinder in the van, which whined and threw up a fine glitter of brass dust. Tilly wrote everything down, including the names of the tools.
The last call came just after lunch, as rain began to drum on the roof. An elderly man stood on the porch of a weatherboard cottage, his cardigan soaked through. Inside, a tabby cat watched him from the windowsill.
'Gerald Abernethy,' he said, shaking Aunt Fen's hand. 'I've been out here an hour. My wife always looked after the spare key. She passed away in March, and I've no idea where she put it.'
Aunt Fen crouched by the door and worked slowly, her head tilted, as if the lock were whispering to her. Tilly watched the rain dripping off Mr Abernethy's nose. Without being asked, she ran back to the van, fetched the big umbrella and held it over him. After a few minutes, there was a small, satisfying click, and the door swung open. The cat strolled out, sniffed Mr Abernethy's shoes and strolled back in again.
Before leaving, Aunt Fen cut two spare keys. 'Don't put one under the mat or in a flowerpot,' she said. 'That's the first place anyone looks. Best to give one to someone you trust who lives close by.'
Mr Abernethy turned the keys over in his palm. 'My wife knew all the neighbours,' he said slowly. 'Had them over for tea. I've let that slide.' He looked across the street. On the porch opposite, a woman was carrying shopping bags inside while a small boy in gumboots stamped in a puddle. The boy saw them and waved.
Mr Abernethy hesitated. Then he raised his hand and waved back, and slipped one of the keys into his cardigan pocket, apart from the other.
In the van, Aunt Fen handed Tilly a peppermint. 'You fetched that umbrella,' she said. 'That's the half that isn't about locks.'

The Case Against the Campfire
Ask most Australians to picture a perfect camping trip and they will describe a crackling fire under the stars. I understand the appeal. I grew up toasting marshmallows over glowing coals. But after many years of camping, I have come to believe that the campfire is a habit we should be ready to give up. A small gas stove does the job better, and it leaves the bush in better shape.
The first problem is risk. A campfire can seem tame, but it takes only one strong gust of wind to carry a burning ember into dry grass. Even after the flames die down, coals can stay hot for many hours. People who cover them with sand or soil often believe they have put the fire out, when they have simply hidden the heat. Fire authorities advise drowning coals with water until they are cold to the touch, yet many campers skip this step when they pack up in a hurry. Every year, rangers find fires still smouldering at sites that campers left that morning.
The second problem is less obvious. Fallen branches and logs are not just untidy leftovers on the forest floor. They are homes. Beetles, spiders, skinks and small marsupials shelter in and under them, while fungi slowly break them down, returning goodness to the soil. When campers gather armfuls of dead wood near a popular campsite, year after year, the ground around it becomes bare. The creatures that relied on that timber must move on or disappear. This is why many national parks now ban the collection of firewood altogether.
A stove avoids both problems. It lights in seconds, boils water quickly and can be switched off completely with a twist of the wrist. It works on rainy evenings when every stick is soaked, and it can be packed away cold within minutes of dinner. There is no smoke in your eyes, and no jumper that smells like a chimney for days afterwards.
I learnt this lesson from my uncle Ray. For twenty years he was a volunteer with the Rural Fire Service, and he spent many summer nights on the fire line. On our family camping trips, my cousins begged him for a bonfire. He never lit one. Instead, he would smile, set up his battered blue stove and put the kettle on. At the time I thought he was simply being boring. Now I think I understand.
I am not asking anyone to give up the joy of camping. The stars still shine, stories can still be told, and hot chocolate tastes just as good from a stove. Next time you head into the bush, try leaving the firewood behind. You may find you miss the fire far less than you expected.

The Planet Behind the Veil
Just after sunset or just before dawn, you may notice a dazzling point of light low in the sky. It shines more brightly than any star, and for thousands of years people called it the 'evening star' or the 'morning star'. In fact, it is not a star at all. It is Venus, the second planet from the Sun and our closest planetary neighbour.
Venus has often been called Earth's twin. The two planets are almost the same size, and they are made of similar rocky material. Early astronomers could not see its surface, because it is hidden beneath a thick blanket of cloud. Some imagined that, under those clouds, there might be warm swamps or steamy jungles full of life.
The truth turned out to be very different. When space probes finally reached Venus in the 1960s and 1970s, they revealed one of the most hostile places in the solar system. The surface temperature is about 465 degrees Celsius, which is hot enough to melt lead. Surprisingly, this makes Venus hotter than Mercury, even though Mercury is much closer to the Sun.
The reason lies in the air. Venus's atmosphere is made almost entirely of carbon dioxide, and it is extremely dense. Sunlight passes through the clouds and warms the ground, but the heat cannot easily escape back into space. Instead, it is trapped by the thick atmosphere, a process known as the greenhouse effect. Mercury, by contrast, has almost no atmosphere, so heat escapes from its surface and the side facing away from the Sun becomes bitterly cold.
The atmosphere of Venus also presses down with tremendous force. Standing on its surface would feel like being nearly a kilometre deep in the ocean. The clouds themselves contain droplets of sulfuric acid, a chemical that can eat away at metal.
Venus is strange in other ways, too. It spins very slowly, and in the opposite direction to most planets. One full turn takes about 243 Earth days, which is longer than the 225 days it takes to travel around the Sun. In other words, a day on Venus is longer than its year.
Several landers sent by the Soviet Union reached the surface between 1970 and 1985. They were built as tough as armoured tanks, yet the heat and pressure silenced each of them within about two hours. The photographs they sent back show a flat, orange-tinted landscape of broken rock.
Scientists are now planning new missions to Venus. They hope to learn how a planet so similar to Earth in size became so different. Understanding what happened to our twin may help us appreciate how fortunate we are to live on a world with mild temperatures and air we can breathe.

ComprehensionText:
The Weaver Who Lit the Sky
Long ago, in a village near the top of the world, winter was a time of endless dark. For two whole months the sun did not rise at all, and the people lived by the glow of their fires and the cold light of the stars. The old ones said that the North Wind sometimes walked among people in disguise, testing whether their hearts were warm or cold.
In that village lived a young weaver named Ylva. Her cloth was the finest for many days' travel, because of her colours. Every summer, while the sun circled the sky day and night, she wandered the hills gathering flowers, berries, lichen and roots. She boiled them in great pots to make her dyes: crimson from cranberries, gold from birch leaves, deep green from moss and a violet that no one else could match. She dipped her wool in them and hung the skeins to dry in the long summer light. Each thread was a summer she had saved.
That year, Ylva wove a cloak from her brightest threads. It shimmered like the sea at sunset, and she meant to wear it to the midwinter gathering, where every eye would turn to her.
Three nights before the gathering, there was a knock at her door. Outside stood a gaunt old man in a grey coat. His beard was white with frost, and when he spoke, his breath turned to ice crystals even in the warmth of her doorway.
'I have travelled far, and the dark has worn me thin,' he said. 'Do you have a scrap of colour to spare?'
Ylva hesitated. Her baskets of thread were nearly empty. All that remained of her summer was the cloak. She thought of the gathering and of everyone admiring her. Then she looked at the old man's tired face, and at the darkness pressing against the windows, and she took the cloak from its hook and placed it in his hands.
He smiled for the first time. 'Generous hearts are rare,' he said, 'rarer than violet dye.' Then he turned and walked into the night. Ylva watched him go. Strangely, though fresh snow covered the path, he left no footprints, and the cloak in his arms rippled and flapped although the air was perfectly still.
On the night of the gathering, the villagers stepped outside and gasped. Across the black sky rippled great curtains of light, green and violet, crimson and gold, folding and unfolding like cloth shaken out in a strong wind. The whole village stood in the snow with faces lifted, glowing with colour.
Ylva did not wear a fine cloak that night. But she stood among her neighbours with her head tipped back, and she knew every one of those colours by name.
To this day, people in the far north say that when the lights dance, the weaver's cloak is being shaken out across the sky, so that no one need face the long dark without a little summer.

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
Living Pantries
In the red sand country of central Australia, rain can stay away for months. Plants wilt, flowers vanish and food for small creatures becomes scarce. Yet deep beneath the mulga scrub, colonies of honeypot ants have a clever way to survive the lean times. They store their food inside the bodies of their own sisters.
Like all ants, honeypot ants live in colonies with a queen and thousands of female workers. Some workers forage above ground. They collect sweet nectar from flowers and honeydew, a sugary liquid produced by tiny sap-sucking insects that feed on mulga trees. But instead of storing this food in wax cells, as bees do, the ants feed it to a special group of workers called repletes.
A replete's job is simply to eat and to wait. Foragers pass liquid into its mouth again and again until its abdomen stretches to many times its normal size. A fully loaded replete can be as large as a grape, its body so swollen that the thin skin between its hard plates becomes almost see-through and glows amber, like a drop of honey. Too heavy to walk, the repletes hang from the ceilings of chambers that may lie more than a metre below the surface, where the soil stays cool and damp.
There they remain, sometimes for months. When the season turns dry and foragers return empty-handed, hungry workers stroke a replete's head with their antennae. In response, it brings up a droplet of stored food and passes it mouth to mouth. In this way a few hundred living storage jars can keep an entire colony alive until the rains return. Scientists believe the repletes may store water as well, which would be just as precious in the desert.
This arrangement is not without risk. A replete cannot run from danger, and a burst replete is food lost for good. The deep, narrow tunnels help protect them, and guard ants patrol the entrances.
Honeypot ants are also important to people. For thousands of years, Aboriginal people of the desert regions have dug for them as a sweet bush food. Finding a nest takes skill: a digger must recognise the small entrance hole, then follow the tunnel down through hard ground, sometimes for a metre or more. The reward is a cluster of golden repletes, which are eaten by biting off the sweet abdomen. Traditionally, diggers leave part of the nest alone so that the colony can recover.
Honeypot ants show that survival does not always depend on being fast, strong or fierce. Sometimes it depends on planning ahead and sharing. A honeypot nest is small, quiet and easy to overlook, yet each one holds a carefully guarded store of sweetness that can last through months of drought.

AnswerC: dangerous to eat

"A principal fruit of friendship," Francis Bacon wrote in his timeless meditation on the subject, "is the ease and discharge of the fulness and swellings of the heart, which passions of all kinds do cause and induce." For Thoreau, friendship was one of life's great rewards. But in today's cultural landscape of muddled relationships scattered across various platforms for connecting, amidst constant debates about whether our Facebook "friendships" are making us more or less happy, it pays to consider what friendship actually is. That's precisely what CUNY philosophy professor Massimo Pigliucci explores in Answers for Aristotle: How Science and Philosophy Can Lead Us to A More Meaningful Life (public library), which also gave us this provocative read on the science of what we call "intuition."

Philosophers and cognitive scientists agree that friendship is an essential ingredient of human happiness. But beyond the dry academic definitions — like, say, "voluntary interdependence between two persons over time, which is intended to facilitate socio-emotional goals of the participants, and may involve varying types and degrees of companionship, intimacy, affection and mutual assistance" — lies a body of compelling research that sheds light on how, precisely, friendship augments happiness.

The way friendship enhances well-being, it turns out, has nothing to do with quantity and everything to do with quality — researchers confirm that it isn't the number of friends (or, in the case of Facebook, "friends")

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
When Words Swap Places
Have you ever meant to say "a crushing blow" and heard yourself say "a blushing crow" instead? If so, you have made a spoonerism: a slip of the tongue in which the first sounds of two words swap places. The result is often nonsense, sometimes oddly poetic, and nearly always funny.
Spoonerisms are named after William Archibald Spooner, a kindly, white-haired teacher at Oxford University in England more than a hundred years ago. Spooner was said to mix up his words so often that his students began collecting his mistakes. He supposedly scolded one lazy student for having "hissed all my mystery lectures", and is said to have told another that he had "tasted a whole worm" when he meant "wasted a whole term". Before long, any such slip was simply called a "spoonerism".
There is just one problem with these famous stories: most of them are probably not true. Spooner admitted to only a few slips, and historians suspect that his students invented many of the best ones, polishing them for laughs and passing them on. Spooner reportedly found his fame rather tiresome. Even so, the name stuck.
Whether Spooner said them or not, slips like these are real, and scientists who study language find them fascinating. When you speak, your brain does not choose one word at a time. It plans several words ahead, lining up the sounds before you say them. Occasionally, a sound from a word that is coming up jumps the queue and lands in the wrong place. That is why spoonerisms almost always swap sounds in matching positions, such as the beginnings of two words, and why the mixed-up result usually still sounds as if it could be English. Even when we make mistakes, our brains follow the rules. Researchers have even caused spoonerisms on purpose in experiments, by flashing pairs of words on a screen and asking volunteers to read them aloud as quickly as possible.
In other words, a spoonerism is not a sign of a careless mind. It is a tiny window into how busy and organised our brains are while we talk.
Spoonerisms have also become a favourite toy for writers and comedians, who make them up on purpose. Here is a limerick built around one:
An usher, with manners so neat,
Met a lady who'd come off the street.
With a bow and a smile
He led her down the aisle,
And said, "Let me sew you to your sheet!"
So if you ever make a spoonerism yourself, there is no need to feel embarrassed. You are in good company. Just smile, correct yourself and carry on. After all, a brain that can swap sounds so neatly is running like a well-boiled icicle.

Even when we make mistakes, our brains follow the rules. Researchers have even caused spoonerisms on purpose in experiments, by flashing pairs of words on a screen and asking volunteers to read them aloud as quickly as possible.
In other words, a spoonerism is not a sign of a careless mind. It is a tiny window into how busy and organised our brains are while we talk.

An usher, with manners so neat,
Met a lady who'd come off the street.
With a bow and a smile
He led her down the aisle,
And said, "Let me sew you to your sheet!"

Mrs Lang's Fairy Books
In 1889, a book with a bright blue cover appeared in London bookshops. The Blue Fairy Book gathered old tales such as "Cinderella", "Rumpelstiltskin" and "Beauty and the Beast", and it sold so well that a Red Fairy Book followed the next year. By 1910 there were twelve volumes, each named after a different colour. Every one carried the same name: Andrew Lang. Yet the person who did most of the writing was barely mentioned.
Leonora Blanche Alleyne was born in 1851 and in 1875 married Andrew Lang, a Scottish scholar and journalist. Andrew was fascinated by folklore and believed fairy tales deserved serious study, not merely a place in the nursery. He was also extraordinarily busy, turning out poems, essays, histories and newspaper columns at a startling pace.
Leonora had a gift for languages. As the fairy book project grew, she took on the task of turning stories from French, German, Spanish, Italian and other languages into lively English. She did not simply translate word for word. She reshaped each tale for young readers, trimming slow passages and softening details that seemed too gruesome for a Victorian nursery. In time she oversaw a small team of translators, most of them women, and polished their work into one consistent voice.
Andrew's role was mainly to choose the stories' themes, write the prefaces and lend his famous name, which helped the books sell. He never pretended to have done everything. In the preface to The Lilac Fairy Book, the final volume, he stated plainly that the books had been almost wholly the work of Mrs Lang. Few readers noticed. The covers did not change, and for generations, children and librarians spoke of "Andrew Lang's fairy books".
Leonora also published books under her own name, including The Red Book of Heroes and The Book of Princes and Princesses. These attracted far less attention than the coloured series.
Why did she stay in the background? Part of the answer lies in the customs of the time. Victorian publishers believed a well-known male author would attract buyers, and many women writers accepted that their work would be credited to someone else. How Leonora herself felt about this is not well recorded.
Today, historians of children's literature are giving her more credit. The coloured fairy books helped decide which tales English-speaking children grew up with, and Leonora's choices about what to keep, what to soften and what to cut still echo through countless picture books and films. She was, in a sense, the invisible gatekeeper of the fairy-tale kingdom.

AnswerD: They believed it would attract more buyers.

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
A Voice in the Shoebox
Four per cent. Tess watched the number on her phone as if staring at it might stop it shrinking. The storm had torn through the valley overnight, and since dawn the farmhouse had been silent: no fridge hum, no lights, no internet. Pop said the power lines were down somewhere near the highway, but nobody knew how long repairs would take.
At three per cent, she switched the phone off and slumped at the kitchen table.
Pop disappeared into the shed and came back with a dusty shoebox. Inside was a tangle of copper wire, a cardboard tube, a tiny glass part no bigger than a grain of rice, and an old earpiece on a cord.
"More junk?" Tess asked.
"A radio," said Pop. "Or it will be, once we build it."
For the next hour they worked side by side. Tess wound the thin wire around the cardboard tube, a hundred careful turns, while Pop scraped the ends bare with his pocketknife. He showed her how to join the tiny glass part, which he called a diode, to the coil and the earpiece. Then they carried a long reel of wire outside, and Pop climbed a ladder to tie one end high up on the windmill. A second wire ran from the shoebox to the metal garden tap.
"Where does the battery go?" Tess asked, searching the box.
"There isn't one," Pop said. "The radio station's tower sends out radio waves day and night, and each wave carries a little energy. By the time they reach us, there's only a whisper of it left, so we need a big net to catch enough. The longer and higher the aerial, the more we catch."
Tess pressed the earpiece to her ear. Nothing. Pop slid a metal clip slowly along the coil. Still nothing, then a crackle, and then, so faint she had to hold her breath, a man's voice.
"...crews are working to restore power to the valley, and supply is expected back by early evening..."
"It's working!" Tess whispered, as if speaking aloud might frighten the voice away. The man was talking from a studio more than a hundred kilometres away, and his words were reaching her through a cardboard tube and some wire, with nothing to power them but the waves themselves.
Just after six, the fridge shuddered back to life and every light in the house came on at once. Tess's phone, charging on the bench, buzzed with a stream of messages.
She didn't look at it. The news had finished, and the announcer was playing an old country song. Tess sat on the back step with the earpiece pressed to her ear, watching the windmill turn slowly against the pink sky, and listened until the very last note.

AnswerB: loud
AnswerC: distant
