Pop disappeared into the shed and came back with a dusty shoebox. Inside was a tangle of copper wire, a cardboard tube, a tiny glass part no bigger than a grain of rice, and an old earpiece on a cord.
"More junk?" Tess asked.
"A radio," said Pop. "Or it will be, once we build it."
For the next hour they worked side by side. Tess wound the thin wire around the cardboard tube, a hundred careful turns, while Pop scraped the ends bare with his pocketknife. He showed her how to join the tiny glass part, which he called a diode, to the coil and the earpiece. Then they carried a long reel of wire outside, and Pop climbed a ladder to tie one end high up on the windmill. A second wire ran from the shoebox to the metal garden tap.
"Where does the battery go?" Tess asked, searching the box.
"There isn't one," Pop said. "The radio station's tower sends out radio waves day and night, and each wave carries a little energy. By the time they reach us, there's only a whisper of it left, so we need a big net to catch enough. The longer and higher the aerial, the more we catch."
Tess pressed the earpiece to her ear. Nothing. Pop slid a metal clip slowly along the coil. Still nothing, then a crackle, and then, so faint she had to hold her breath, a man's voice.
"...crews are working to restore power to the valley, and supply is expected back by early evening..."
"It's working!" Tess whispered, as if speaking aloud might frighten the voice away. The man was talking from a studio more than a hundred kilometres away, and his words were reaching her through a cardboard tube and some wire, with nothing to power them but the waves themselves.
Just after six, the fridge shuddered back to life and every light in the house came on at once. Tess's phone, charging on the bench, buzzed with a stream of messages.
She didn't look at it. The news had finished, and the announcer was playing an old country song. Tess sat on the back step with the earpiece pressed to her ear, watching the windmill turn slowly against the pink sky, and listened until the very last note.
QuestionText: What is the main reason the author begins the story with Tess watching her phone battery run down?
AnswerA: to show how bored Tess felt during the blackout
AnswerB: to set up a contrast with a radio that needs no battery
AnswerC: to suggest that Tess was careless with her things
AnswerD: to explain why the storm had cut off the power

The Month Without Wrappers
It was Mum's idea, which was the first warning sign. 'For the whole of July,' she announced at dinner, 'this family is going plastic-free.'
Dad said, 'Right,' in the voice he used for things he planned to forget. My brother Sami, who is nine, asked whether that included Lego. I said nothing, because I was fourteen and had learned that the best way to survive Mum's projects was to wait for them to collapse on their own.
The first week was chaos. You don't realise how much plastic there is until you try to avoid it. Bread came in plastic bags. Cheese came in plastic. Even the bamboo toothbrushes Mum ordered online arrived in a plastic sleeve, which she held up at breakfast like evidence in a court case. Sami's lunch box, normally a cheerful pile of little packets, became a stern arrangement of apple slices and a cheese sandwich in a beeswax wrap that smelled faintly of candles. He swapped it for a muesli bar on the first day and got caught.
I started keeping a list of every failure so I could read it out at the end, like a reporter. Then Nana came to stay.
Nana grew up on a dairy farm near Bega in the 1950s, and she watched our battle with the bread bags for about two days before she quietly took over. She showed Mum how to ask the bakery to drop loaves straight into a cotton bag. She made yoghurt in a glass jar wrapped in a tea towel on the bench. She taught Sami to bake crackers, which he decided were better than the packet ones, mostly because he was allowed to cut them into dinosaur shapes. She remembered milk in glass bottles with foil caps that birds pecked through, and a grocer who wrapped everything in newspaper. 'We weren't trying to save the planet,' she said. 'We just didn't have the other stuff yet.'
She took me with her to the bulk-food shop on Saturday, where you fill your own containers from big bins of oats, lentils and nuts. I expected it to be boring. Instead it was oddly satisfying, like a cross between a library and a lolly shop. Nana weighed the empty jars first so the cashier could subtract them, and the man behind the counter knew her name by the second visit.
By the end of July, we were not plastic-free. Not even close. Medicine still came in blister packs, Dad never found a shampoo he liked, and Sami's Lego remained a protected species. But our yellow recycling bin, which used to overflow every fortnight, was only half full, and the red bin was lighter too.
At the final dinner, Mum asked what we had learned. I had my failure list in my pocket, three pages long. I didn't read it out. Instead I said we should keep the bulk-shop trips going, and maybe the yoghurt.
Nana smiled into her cup of tea. Later I found the list still folded in my pocket, and on the back I started a different one: things we could actually keep doing. It was shorter. But it was the kind of list you can stick on a fridge.

AnswerA: the narrator expected the project to fall apart on its own
AnswerB: the narrator was too excited about the plan to speak
AnswerC: the narrator did not understand what plastic-free meant
AnswerD: the narrator was waiting for Nana to arrive and decide

ComprehensionText:
Give the Tricksters Their Due
Ask most students to name a character from mythology and you will probably hear about a hero: Hercules wrestling a lion, perhaps, or Perseus with his mirrored shield. Heroes dominate the posters, the films and the school units. I think that is a pity, because the most useful characters in the world's myths are not the heroes at all. They are the tricksters, and it is time they were given a proper place in our classrooms.
A trickster is a clever, mischievous figure who wins by wit rather than strength. Almost every culture has one. In West Africa and the Caribbean, Anansi the spider outwits creatures far larger than himself. In Polynesian stories, Maui snares the sun with ropes and slows it down so that his people have longer days. In Norse myth, Loki stirs up chaos and then, as often as not, has to fix it. North American peoples tell of Coyote, and Japanese folktales feature a shape-shifting fox. The fact that so many cultures, separated by oceans, created such similar characters should make us curious. They must be telling us something people everywhere needed to hear.
So what do tricksters teach? First, they show that brains can beat brawn. Most of us will never wrestle a lion, but all of us will face problems that need creative solutions. A hero's answer is usually to be stronger; a trickster's answer is to think differently. That is a lesson worth more than any amount of sword-swinging.
Second, tricksters are honest about failure. Heroes rarely make mistakes, which makes them hard to relate to. Tricksters, on the other hand, are forever getting caught in their own traps. Anansi's greed lands him in trouble again and again. Readers laugh, but they also learn that cleverness without good judgement can backfire. I can think of no better lesson for a teenager.
Third, trickster tales are funny, and humour is a powerful aid to memory. Students who yawn through a list of ancient kings will happily retell the story of how a spider persuaded a python to stretch out beside a branch to settle an argument about its length, then tied it up.
Some people argue that tricksters are poor role models because they lie and cheat. I understand the worry, but it misreads the stories. Nobody finishes an Anansi tale wanting to copy his greed; they finish it understanding where greed leads. Myths have never been simple instruction manuals. They are invitations to think.
I am not asking schools to throw out Hercules. Heroes have their place, and their courage is worth admiring. But if we only ever teach the strong, we send students the message that problems are solved by force and that winners are people who never stumble. The tricksters tell a truer story: that the small can outsmart the mighty, that mistakes are part of learning, and that a good laugh can carry wisdom across a thousand years. Let's give them their due.

ComprehensionText:
Water Uphill to Kalgoorlie
In 1892, prospectors found gold at Coolgardie, in the dry country more than five hundred kilometres east of Perth. A year later, an Irish prospector named Paddy Hannan made another find nearby, at what became Kalgoorlie. Tens of thousands of people rushed to the area hoping to make their fortunes. They found gold, but they also found one of the harshest environments in Australia. Rain was scarce and unreliable, there were no permanent rivers, and the little groundwater available was often too salty to drink.
Water quickly became more precious than the gold itself. It was carted in on camels, collected in tanks, or produced by condensers that boiled salty water and captured the steam. In hot summers, a bucket of water could cost more than a meal. Without clean water, diseases such as typhoid spread through the crowded camps, and many people died.
The government of Western Australia turned to its Engineer-in-Chief, Charles Yelverton O'Connor, who had already built the harbour at Fremantle. His plan was astonishing for its time. He proposed building a dam on the Helena River in the hills near Perth and pumping water through a pipeline about 530 kilometres long to the goldfields. The difficulty was not only the distance. Kalgoorlie stands about 400 metres higher than the dam, so the water would have to be pushed uphill most of the way.
Many people thought the idea was impossible or wasteful. Newspapers mocked it, and some politicians argued that the gold might run out before the pipeline was finished, leaving the colony with an enormous debt and a pipe to nowhere. O'Connor and the Premier, John Forrest, held firm, and work began in 1898.
The project used new technology. Instead of riveting the steel pipes, engineers used a locking-bar method that clamped the edges of each pipe together, making the joints stronger and less likely to leak. Thousands of workers laid the pipes in the summer heat, and eight steam-driven pumping stations were built along the route to lift the water in stages.
In January 1903, the water reached Kalgoorlie, and crowds celebrated as it gushed into a reservoir on the edge of town. O'Connor did not see that day. He died in 1902, less than a year before the opening, after years of fierce public criticism. Today he is remembered as one of the country's great engineers.
The goldfields boomed after the water arrived. Towns gained gardens, parks and swimming pools, and the mining industry could expand with confidence. The pipeline, later extended to farms and towns across the Wheatbelt, still operates more than a century later, though electric pumps have replaced the old steam engines. In 2009 it was recognised as an International Historic Civil Engineering Landmark, an honour it shares with structures such as the Eiffel Tower and the Panama Canal.
The pipeline changed what people believed was possible in the Australian interior. It showed that, with enough vision and determination, even a desert town could be given a reliable supply of water.

A year later, an Irish prospector named Paddy Hannan made another find nearby, at what became Kalgoorlie. Tens of thousands of people rushed to the area hoping to make their fortunes. They found gold, but they also found one of the harshest environments in Australia. Rain was scarce and unreliable, there were no permanent rivers, and the little groundwater available was often too salty to drink.
Water quickly became more precious than the gold itself. It was carted in on camels, collected in tanks, or produced by condensers that boiled salty water and captured the steam. In hot summers, a bucket of water could cost more than a meal. Without clean water, diseases such as typhoid spread through the crowded camps, and many people died.
The government of Western Australia turned to its Engineer-in-Chief, Charles Yelverton O'Connor, who had already built the harbour at Fremantle. His plan was astonishing for its time. He proposed building a dam on the Helena River in the hills near Perth and pumping water through a pipeline about 530 kilometres long to the goldfields. The difficulty was not only the distance. Kalgoorlie stands about 400 metres higher than the dam, so the water would have to be pushed uphill most of the way.
Many people thought the idea was impossible or wasteful. Newspapers mocked it, and some politicians argued that the gold might run out before the pipeline was finished, leaving the colony with an enormous debt and a pipe to nowhere. O'Connor and the Premier, John Forrest, held firm, and work began in 1898.
The project used new technology. Instead of riveting the steel pipes, engineers used a locking-bar method that clamped the edges of each pipe together, making the joints stronger and less likely to leak. Thousands of workers laid the pipes in the summer heat, and eight steam-driven pumping stations were built along the route to lift the water in stages.
In January 1903, the water reached Kalgoorlie, and crowds celebrated as it gushed into a reservoir on the edge of town. O'Connor did not see that day. He died in 1902, less than a year before the opening, after years of fierce public criticism. Today he is remembered as one of the country's great engineers.
The goldfields boomed after the water arrived. Towns gained gardens, parks and swimming pools, and the mining industry could expand with confidence. The pipeline, later extended to farms and towns across the Wheatbelt, still operates more than a century later, though electric pumps have replaced the old steam engines. In 2009 it was recognised as an International Historic Civil Engineering Landmark, an honour it shares with structures such as the Eiffel Tower and the Panama Canal.
The pipeline changed what people believed was possible in the Australian interior. It showed that, with enough vision and determination, even a desert town could be given a reliable supply of water.

ComprehensionText:
Teaching Your Budgie to Step Up
Budgerigars, or budgies, are small Australian parrots that have become one of the most popular pets in the world. In the wild they fly in large, chattering flocks across the inland, so a single budgie in a cage can easily become bored and lonely. Training is one of the best ways to keep a pet budgie's mind busy, and the first skill most owners teach is the 'step up', in which the bird hops onto your finger when asked. This guide explains how to teach it safely.
What you will need
- a quiet room with the windows and doors closed and any ceiling fans switched off
- a supply of millet spray, a seed treat most budgies adore
- a short, smooth perch or a clean wooden chopstick
- patience: some birds learn in a week, while others take a month or more
Before you begin
A budgie brought home from a pet shop or breeder needs time to settle. For at least the first week, do not try to handle it. Instead, sit beside the cage each day and talk softly so the bird grows used to your voice and presence. Budgies are prey animals, and in the wild a shape swooping from above could mean a hungry hawk. Rushing this stage can leave a bird nervous of hands for life.
Step 1: Hand in the cage
Rest your hand quietly inside the cage, near but not touching the bird, for a few minutes at a time. Hold a piece of millet between your fingers. At first your budgie may flutter away, but over several sessions it will usually edge closer to nibble the treat. Do not grab at it.
Step 2: Offer a finger
Once your budgie eats calmly from your hand, slide one finger slowly towards it, just above its feet. Approach from the side or below, never from directly overhead. Say 'step up' in a clear, cheerful tone as you press very gently against its lower chest. Most budgies will lift a foot to keep their balance. The moment both feet are on your finger, reward the bird with millet and praise.
Step 3: Practise and progress
Keep sessions short, about five to ten minutes, and finish while your budgie is still keen. A tired or frightened bird will start to puff, pant or flap, which is a sign to stop. Repeat the command using exactly the same words each time. When your budgie steps up reliably inside the cage, you can try carrying it a short distance out of the cage.
Troubleshooting
If your bird bites, do not jerk your hand away, as this teaches it that biting works. Hold still, stay calm and try again later. If your budgie is afraid of fingers, offer the perch or chopstick instead; many birds feel safer stepping onto wood. If your budgie seems uninterested, try a session shortly before its usual feeding time, when a millet reward will seem far more tempting.
A well-trained budgie is a happier, more confident companion. The chirps and chatter you hear at the end of a successful session are your reward for all that patience.

'Stock,' he said. 'Start again.'
Jaya felt her face go hot. She nearly untied her apron there and then. Instead, she grabbed another onion and attacked it, harder this time, determined not to give him the satisfaction of seeing her quit.
'Stop.' He was beside her again. This time he did not take the board away. He put his large hand over hers and tilted the knife so the tip rested on the board. He showed her, his knuckles guiding the side of the blade. 'Cut the root last. The root holds it together, and it holds the tears in too.'
She tried it. The slices came out thin and even. He grunted, which she would later learn was the closest he came to praise, and went back to his pot.

By the twentieth onion, she had found a rhythm. By the thirtieth, her eyes had almost stopped stinging. By the fortieth, the smell of onions softening in oil filled the hall, and people had begun to line up outside.

'He made me do the onions too,' Rosa said, ladling stew into a bowl. 'Everyone does the onions on their first day. Half of them never come back.'
'Why does he do it?'
Rosa shrugged. 'He says if you can't be patient with an onion, you won't be patient with people.' She nodded at the queue, where an elderly man was slowly counting out coins he did not need to pay. 'And people here need patience more than anything.'
Jaya watched the man carry his bowl to a corner table and close his eyes as the steam rose into his face. Somewhere in that stew were her forty onions.
The following Saturday, she arrived ten minutes early. Mr Okafor looked up from the stove, glanced at her apron, and almost smiled.
'Carrots,' he said.

A Lasting Impact Scarlett looked on with pride as she observed a fellow eighth grader casually walk over to one of the many recycling bins at school to dispose of an empty water bottle. As the new president of the school recycling club, Scarlett had played a big part in increasing awareness about the importance of recycling items properly. She and the other members of the club had worked together to make sure that a recycling bin was in every public area at the school. "A simple action that has a lasting impact" was the slogan the members of the recycling club had placed on each bin, reminding students that disposing of recyclable items was an easy task that could have a profound effect on the environment. The school year had just begun, and Scarlett was already thinking about activities to encourage students to be more enthusiastic about recycling. As the president of the recycling club, she wanted to surpass the recycling record the school had set the previous year. The school had recycled an amazing amount of trash for the past five years, and she hoped this year would be even better. Scarlett went home at the end of the day, feeling optimistic about the school year. She sat down at her computer and looked online, hoping to find inspiration for events the club could organize at school. Instead, she uncovered some alarming information that quickly swept away her positive attitude. During her research, she learned that electronic waste, or e-waste as it is commonly called, represents about 2 percent of trash in landfills. No-longer-used computers, cell phones, and televisions are just a few examples of this type of waste. Unfortunately, as companies that produce these items continue to improve upon technology and people replace existing electronics with newer, better versions, the amount of e-waste that is created will only increase. Scarlett was disappointed in herself for not taking action to bring awareness to this problem sooner. At that moment, she began to develop a plan. The next day at school, Scarlett was on a mission. There was one person who would definitely be able to help the recycling club bring attention to this cause. "Hey, Juan Carlos," Scarlett beamed as she saw her friend in the hallway. "How would you like to make your last year of middle school a real success?" Juan Carlos gave a questioning look before Scarlett outlined her plan. It didn't take much for Juan Carlos to agree to help even though he was not a member of the club. Next, Scarlett went to find Mr. Rhomberg, the recycling club sponsor, to receive approval. If she could convince him that this endeavor was worth pursuing, she knew the plan would be put into place soon. "There is a special project I want us to work on this year," Scarlett announced at that week's recycling club meeting. "We have all heard about e-waste, but I recently learned the enormous impact it's having on our environment." She went on to tell the club members that she wanted to organize a drive to collect e-waste there at the school. In the next few months, the recycling club would organize an e-waste drive—a day when students and their families could drop off unwanted electronics to be recycled. A local recycling company would pick up the items to dispose of them properly. "I'm sure you've all noticed that we have a visitor here today," Scarlett said as she pointed to Juan Carlos. "He's going to help us with the graphics to promote our drive." The members responded to the news positively, since Juan Carlos was known for his artistic ability. "His drawings will be featured on flyers and in our school newsletter, which will include a special section about the upcoming drive. Now let's get to work!"

For several weeks, the recycling club planned the upcoming e-waste drive, or e-drive as it was soon called. Flyers were placed around the school, references were made during morning announcements, and science classes welcomed a guest speaker from a local recycling company to inform students about e-waste.

The big day finally arrived, and Scarlett was nervous. She and the other members of the recycling club arrived at school early that Saturday morning to make sure that everything went smoothly. Since this was going to be a large event, the local recycling company that the school had been working with agreed to haul away any electronic items that were collected that day. Scarlett learned that many local organizations accept e-waste daily, so Juan Carlos created a large poster with the names and locations of those organizations to remind people that proper disposal of electronics was something that could be done any time of the year. Everyone waited in anticipation, hoping that students at the school would participate in the event.

It wasn't long before the first cars pulled into the school parking lot. After several minutes, more people arrived. Before long, Scarlett and the other members were hurrying back and forth, helping people as they carried their electronics for recycling to the designated places in the gymnasium. Phones, computers, keyboards, and TVs soon began piling up in huge stacks. As Scarlett helped, she heard someone suggest that the school have another e-drive in a few months. Scarlett smiled, knowing that a simple action could truly have a lasting impact.

The following passage is an extract from Coming of Age as a Mexican American Woman by Frances Esquibel Tywoniak and Mario T.García.

I especially remember my English classes with great affection. Part of my excitement about these classes had to do with my teachers. My freshman^1 English teacher, for example, was very lively. She was a round-faced twinkle-eyed woman who seemed to care about her students. For instance, she noticed that at first my mind would sometimes wander. I would daydream a bit because I was still getting over Peter. When she observed this, she would gently bring me back to reality in some wonderful creative way without making me feel guilty. 'If I could just have your attention, Frances,' she might say. Startled out of some reverie, I would look in her direction to find a knowing but gentle look of understanding on her face. Her smile made it seem all right.

In this way she won my trust and thereby won me over to her love of literature. In her class, Shakespeare came alive. Portia was a real person. So was Shylock. Even grammar was exciting. Grammar clarified and refined language. There was a reason for it. Adjectives and adverbs had a purpose. That purpose was the beauty of language.

I found that I was responding to both close teacher direction and to being given latitude to work on my own. One teacher to whom I responded very well and whom I very much admired was Miss Julien, another one of my English teachers. She was rumoured to be a Communist. I didn't know what a Communist was. What I did know was that she was a wonderful teacher. She ran her classes very differently. She would have us do our work independently and look up the answers and figure things out on our own. She didn't spoon-feed us. Grammar drill sheets with correct answers didn't count.

'Teach yourselves,' she would say. 'Learn how to learn.' She wanted to know what we were thinking. What counted, she said, was our ability to write with clarity.

I responded to her encouragement, as did the other students. There was no fooling around in Miss Julien's class.

AnswerA: did not believe in only one right answer.

Designing an Alien That Makes Sense
Science fiction is full of aliens that are really just people in rubber masks: two arms, two legs, a lumpy forehead and a bad attitude. If you want readers to believe in your creature, you need to think like a scientist before you think like an artist. This guide shows you how to build an alien from the ground up, starting not with the creature but with its world.
What you will need
A notebook, a pencil, some basic knowledge of how living things on Earth survive, and a willingness to throw away your first idea.
Step 1: Choose the planet first
Every living thing is shaped by its surroundings, so begin there. Decide how big your planet is, because size affects gravity. On a large, heavy world, gravity pulls harder, so tall, spindly creatures would struggle; short, broad bodies with thick legs make more sense. On a small world with weak gravity, tall and delicate shapes become possible. Write down whether the planet is hot or cold, wet or dry, and whether it has seasons.
Step 2: Look at the light
Next, think about the star your planet orbits. Many stars are smaller, cooler and redder than our Sun. Under a dim red sun, plants might be dark, even black, to soak up as much light as possible, and animals might have huge eyes, or senses that do not rely on sight at all. On a world wrapped in thick cloud, hearing or smell could matter far more than vision.
Step 3: Decide what it eats and what eats it
A creature's body is a record of how it gets food and avoids becoming food. Hunters on Earth often have eyes facing forward to judge distance, while hunted animals often have eyes on the sides of their heads to watch for danger. Ask the same questions about your alien. Does it chase, graze, filter or trap? What is it afraid of?
Step 4: Give every feature a reason
Now sketch the body, but justify each part. If it has six legs, why? If it is covered in plates, what are they protecting it from? A useful rule is that if you cannot explain a feature, cut it. The best alien designs feel strange at first and then, a moment later, feel inevitable.
Step 5: Test it with a story
Finally, drop your creature into a short scene. Have it hunt, hide, raise young or survive a storm. Problems will appear quickly. Perhaps its delicate wings would be shredded by the planet's fierce winds, or it has no way to stay cool in the long summer. Go back and adjust. Designers of films and games often go through dozens of versions before they settle on one.
Common mistakes
The most common mistake is making an alien too human. Another is giving it features simply because they look frightening, such as rows of teeth on a creature that eats only moss. Readers notice these things, even if they cannot say why.
Remember, an alien is not a monster with a costume on. It is the answer to a question your planet has asked. Get the question right, and the answer will almost design itself.

AnswerB: Step 1
AnswerC: Step 4

The Box That Isn't Black
When an aircraft crashes anywhere in the world, investigators immediately begin searching for two devices: the flight data recorder and the cockpit voice recorder. Together they are often called the 'black box', although neither of them is black. Both are painted a vivid orange so that they can be spotted among wreckage, mud or seaweed. Remarkably, the idea behind them came from a young Australian scientist working in a Melbourne laboratory in the 1950s.
David Warren had a personal reason to care about air safety. When he was a boy, his father was among the passengers on the aircraft Miss Hobart, which disappeared over Bass Strait in 1934. No trace of what went wrong was ever found.
In 1953, Warren was a chemist at the Aeronautical Research Laboratories when he was asked to help explain a series of crashes involving the Comet, the world's first jet airliner. The investigators had almost nothing to go on. Warren remembered a pocket-sized recorder he had seen at a trade fair and began to wonder. What if every aircraft carried a device that recorded the pilots' voices and the readings of the instruments? Investigators would no longer have to guess.
His superiors were unconvinced. Some officials argued that the device would be of no use to the people actually flying the aircraft, and pilots objected that it would be like having a spy in the cockpit. Warren kept working on the idea, often in his own time, and by 1958 he had built a prototype that stored four hours of speech and instrument readings on a reel of steel wire.
The breakthrough came from overseas. A visiting British aviation official saw the prototype and arranged for Warren to demonstrate it in London, where it attracted enormous interest. Back home, attitudes shifted after a passenger aircraft crashed near Mackay in Queensland in 1960 and investigators could not establish the cause. The inquiry recommended that recorders be fitted to airliners, and Australia later became the first country to make cockpit voice recorders compulsory.
Modern recorders look very different from Warren's wire-reel machine. They store information on memory chips and can track hundreds, sometimes thousands, of measurements, such as altitude, speed and engine temperature. The memory is sealed inside a casing designed to survive a tremendous impact, intense fire and the crushing pressure of deep water. Each recorder also carries a beacon that sends out signals underwater for weeks, helping searchers find it on the sea floor.
The true value of the black box lies less in explaining any single accident than in preventing the next one. When investigators learn that a part failed or a warning was misunderstood, manufacturers can redesign the part and airlines can retrain their crews. Each lesson is shared across the industry, which is one reason flying is now among the safest ways to travel. Warren, who died in 2010, lived to see his invention carried by airliners all over the world. A boy who had lost his father to an unexplained crash had given the world a way to make sure fewer questions went unanswered.

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
Three Days on the Bibbulmun
Friday 12 April, Mount Cooke campsite
Aunt Jo says keeping a diary will help me 'notice things'. So far I have noticed that my pack weighs eleven kilograms, that my left boot rubs, and that there is no phone reception anywhere in the jarrah forest. The Bibbulmun Track runs for about a thousand kilometres, from the hills outside Perth all the way to Albany, and Jo wants to walk the whole thing next spring. This weekend is her 'practice run'. I am, apparently, her practice companion. She has planned everything: dehydrated meals, a stove the size of a coffee cup, three litres of water each and a paper map in a zip-lock bag in case the markers are hard to find.
We followed the yellow triangle markers all day. At the top of Mount Cooke there were granite slabs warm from the sun, and forest rolled away in every direction like a green ocean. I didn't say anything, but I took a photo. Then I remembered I couldn't send it to anyone.
The campsite has a three-sided timber shelter, a water tank and a toilet, which Jo calls luxury. We wrote our names in the logbook, which every walker is supposed to sign so rangers know who is on the track.
Saturday 13 April, Nerang campsite
I woke at 5.40 because a kookaburra had decided our shelter was a stage. Jo was already boiling water for porridge. She asked if I'd slept well. I said the floor was like sleeping on a chopping board, which was true, but I had actually slept better than I have in weeks.
Today was shorter but hillier. My blister got worse, so Jo showed me how to tape it before it burst. She has a little kit with everything in it: tape, a needle, antiseptic, even a tiny pair of scissors. She told me she once walked on a blister for two days without stopping to fix it and ended up limping for a week. 'The bush doesn't care how tough you are,' she said. 'Fix small problems while they're small.'
In the afternoon we didn't talk for almost an hour. It wasn't awkward. I listened to the wind moving through the treetops and to some birds Jo said were western rosellas. I realised I hadn't thought about the science test once. That night we ate pasta out of the pot and watched the stars come out between the branches.
Sunday 14 April, back at the car
Last entry. My legs ache in places I didn't know had muscles. We walked out this morning through mist so thick the trees looked like grey ghosts, and then the sun burned through and everything sparkled. On the drive home I asked Jo why she had really invited me, since she clearly didn't need any help. She kept her eyes on the road and said that at Christmas I had looked 'like someone who needed more sky'. I didn't know what to say, so I said nothing.
I have already checked the track website. There is a section through the karri forest near Pemberton where the trees are taller than a fifteen-storey building. Jo says that if I keep the blister tape in my pack, I can come.
I told her I'd think about it. I've already thought about it.

AnswerB: too expensive for most walkers
AnswerC: crowded with other hikers

Exhibit Twelve

My granddaughter tugs me past the steam engines.
She's nine, and walks the way she reads, too fast,
skipping the boring bits to reach the end,
past the cases of valves and coiled copper wire,
to a corner where an orange arm stands bolted to the floor,
its elbow bent, its wrist cocked like a question.
'Look, Nanna,' she says. 'A robot.' The sign reads
WELDING ARM, 1984. GIFT OF KESTREL MOTOR WORKS.
I know, I tell her. I used to work beside it.

It came the winter I turned thirty,
crated like a piano, unpacked like a prince.
The foreman called us round to watch it move.
It swung, it dipped, it touched the seam with light,
and where its fingertip had kissed the steel
a weld ran neat as stitching on a Sunday shirt.
Nobody clapped. We knew what it could count.

For eleven years we shared the line, that arm and I.
It never asked for smoko, never hummed,
never brought a thermos or a photo of its kids.
It did four hundred welds an hour, each one the same,
while I did fewer, and each one was mine:
a little thick here, a little proud there,
the way a signature is never quite repeated.

At smoko we would sit along the wall
with sandwiches and crosswords and the radio,
and watch it working on right through our break,
not tired, not bored, not anything at all.
Big Col would raise his mug to it and say,
'Cheers, mate, have one on us,' and we would laugh
the way you laugh at weather you can't change.

People ask me now if I hated it.
I tell them hate is for things that can choose.
It didn't choose to come. It didn't take my job;
somebody signed a paper in an office far away,
and the arm just went on welding, innocent as rain,
the same week they handed us our envelopes,
a handshake and a clock with a brass plate.

Still, I'll admit, on bad nights I would dream it
swinging toward me down an empty line,
its single eye of light gone cold and searching,
and I would wake and hear the fridge, and think
of all the hands that used to make that sound,
the clink and hiss and shout of forty people
turned into one long, perfect, patient hum.

My granddaughter presses the button on the rail.
The arm lifts, turns and slowly bows to her,
a little stiff, the way my knees are now.
She laughs and waves. She builds robots at school,
small ones, from kits, that follow a black line
across the classroom floor and win her ribbons.
She tells me how the sensors read the floor,
how every move begins as lines of code
that she can change whenever something's wrong.
She wants to make one that can help old people walk.

And here's the thing I never thought I'd feel:
I'm proud of her, and not one bit afraid.
The arm and I are both museum pieces now,
both pensioned off, both slower than we were.
Maybe the question never was the arm,
but whose hands plan the work, and what it's for.
And hers, I think, are good hands for the job.

AnswerA: lifted into place by a crane
AnswerB: painted in bright factory colours
AnswerC: checked carefully by experts
AnswerD: packed in a large wooden box

It didn't choose to come. It didn't take my job;
somebody signed a paper in an office far away,
and the arm just went on welding, innocent as rain,
the same week they handed us our envelopes,
a handshake and a clock with a brass plate.

Still, I'll admit, on bad nights I would dream it
swinging toward me down an empty line,
its single eye of light gone cold and searching,
and I would wake and hear the fridge, and think
of all the hands that used to make that sound,
the clink and hiss and shout of forty people
turned into one long, perfect, patient hum.

My granddaughter presses the button on the rail.
The arm lifts, turns and slowly bows to her,
a little stiff, the way my knees are now.
She laughs and waves. She builds robots at school,
small ones, from kits, that follow a black line
across the classroom floor and win her ribbons.
She tells me how the sensors read the floor,
how every move begins as lines of code
that she can change whenever something's wrong.
She wants to make one that can help old people walk.

And here's the thing I never thought I'd feel:
I'm proud of her, and not one bit afraid.
The arm and I are both museum pieces now,
both pensioned off, both slower than we were.
Maybe the question never was the arm,
but whose hands plan the work, and what it's for.
And hers, I think, are good hands for the job.

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
The Moths That Follow the Stars
Every spring, as the weather warms, millions of brown moths set off on one of the most remarkable journeys made by any insect. Bogong moths, each with a body barely as long as a paperclip, fly up to a thousand kilometres from the plains of southern Queensland, New South Wales and western Victoria to the Australian Alps. There they crowd into cool caves and rock crevices near the mountain tops, sometimes packed so tightly that the walls appear to be covered in brown roof tiles.
The moths travel to escape the heat. Summer on the plains is too hot and dry for them, so instead of feeding and breeding they spend the warm months resting in the cool mountain air, in a state of reduced activity similar to hibernation. When autumn arrives, they fly all the way back to the plains, where they mate, lay their eggs and die. The following spring, a new generation of moths, none of which has ever seen the mountains, makes the same journey to the same caves.
How they find their way has puzzled scientists for decades. The moths fly at night, so they cannot rely on landmarks in the way that many birds do. Research has shown that they can sense the Earth's magnetic field, and recent studies have found that they also use the pattern of stars in the night sky as a compass. When city lights or thick cloud hide the stars, the moths can become confused. In some years, swarms have drifted off course into the bright lights of Canberra and even Sydney.
For such small creatures, Bogong moths punch well above their weight in the alpine ecosystem. Their bodies are rich in fat, so the moths arriving each spring deliver a huge supply of energy to the mountains. Birds, lizards and small mammals feast on them. One animal depends on them more than any other: the endangered mountain pygmy possum, which wakes from its winter hibernation hungry and relies heavily on the moths to rebuild its strength before breeding. For thousands of years, Aboriginal peoples also travelled to the high country in summer to gather the moths, roasting them as a rich and nourishing food.
In recent years, however, the journey has become far less crowded. Between 2017 and 2019, the number of moths reaching the caves dropped dramatically, and some caves that once held huge numbers were almost empty. Scientists believe that severe drought on the plains reduced the plants that the caterpillars feed on, so fewer moths survived to make the trip. During those years, researchers reported that mountain pygmy possums in some areas struggled to raise their young. In 2021, the Bogong moth was listed as endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
Researchers now monitor the caves each year, and some communities encourage people to switch off unnecessary outdoor lights during the migration season. The Bogong moth is a reminder that the health of a mountain can depend on events hundreds of kilometres away, and on a creature small enough to sit on your fingertip.

AnswerA: the Bogong moth's migration and why it matters
AnswerB: the habits of the mountain pygmy possum
AnswerC: how insects survive in the heat of summer
AnswerD: the caves and rock crevices of the Alps

Treasure from the Roadside
Most artists build their careers in their twenties and thirties. Rosalie Gascoigne held her first solo exhibition at the age of fifty-seven, using materials that most people would have driven straight past: weathered road signs, broken soft-drink crates, rusty iron and the feathers of swans. Within a few years, she was one of the most admired artists in Australia.
Gascoigne was born in Auckland, New Zealand, in 1917. In 1943 she married an astronomer, Ben Gascoigne, and moved with him to Mount Stromlo Observatory, on a hilltop outside Canberra. It was a lonely place for a young mother. The observatory was isolated, the community was small, and the dry, windswept paddocks looked nothing like the green hills of her childhood. For years she felt like a stranger in the landscape.
Her way of coming to terms with it was to walk. While her husband studied the stars, she explored the grasslands of the Monaro and the roadsides around Canberra, bringing home things that caught her eye: smooth stones, sheep bones, dried thistles, sheets of rusted corrugated iron. She began arranging them, at first simply to decorate the house. In the 1960s she studied ikebana, the Japanese art of flower arranging, which taught her to think carefully about line, space and balance.
Gradually her arrangements became something more. She started to create assemblages, works made by combining found objects. She never painted the landscape directly. Instead she tried to capture how it felt: the glare of the light on dry grass, the rhythm of fence posts, the way a paddock looks from a moving car. In one well-known work, she pushed hundreds of swan feathers into a wire fence frame, so that it seemed to shimmer like a flock in flight.
Her most famous works used old road signs. Gascoigne collected them from tips and roadsides, cut them into strips and squares, then rearranged the pieces in grids. Letters were broken up so the words no longer made sense, and what remained were patterns of bright yellow, black and white. Viewers often say these works suggest sunlight flickering across fields or the endless repetition of a country road.
Recognition came quickly once it began. Galleries bought her work, and in 1982 she was chosen to represent Australia at the Venice Biennale, one of the world's most important art events. Yet she never stopped scavenging. Friends remembered her roaming the tips with a sharp eye, delighted by a faded plank or a sun-bleached sign that nobody else wanted.
Gascoigne died in 1999, but her work remains in major galleries across Australia. Her story is often told as one of a late beginning, and it is that. It is also a story about looking. She spent decades in a landscape that at first seemed empty and harsh to her, and by paying close attention to it, and to the things others had thrown away, she found beauty that had been there all along.

Nobody Invited Them
In August 1947, a grand new arts festival opened in Edinburgh, Scotland. Its organisers had invited orchestras, opera companies and famous theatre groups from across Europe. But eight small theatre companies that had not been invited turned up anyway. Rather than going home, they found whatever spaces they could and put on their shows around the edges of the official program. A local writer described their efforts as happening on the 'fringe' of the festival, and the name stuck.
Those uninvited performers started something remarkable. Today, the Edinburgh Festival Fringe is one of the largest arts festivals on the planet, with thousands of shows each August staged in theatres, school halls, cafes, lecture rooms and even a double-decker bus. Its central rule is simple: there is no selection panel. If you can find a venue and pay the registration fee, you can perform.
Australia has embraced the idea. The Adelaide Fringe began in 1960 and is now the largest arts festival in the Southern Hemisphere. During February and March, the city is transformed. Comedians perform in shipping containers, jugglers fill the parks, and a magician might share a laneway with a string quartet.
I believe the open-door model is the best way to run a festival, and our school's annual arts night should adopt it.
At the moment, a committee of teachers chooses which acts will perform. The committee does a careful job, but the result is predictable. The same confident students, usually those who already take music or drama lessons, appear every year. Plenty of talented people never audition because they assume they will not be picked.
A fringe removes that barrier. Without a panel deciding who is good enough, performers take risks. Some shows will be brilliant, some will be odd and a few may fall flat. That is part of the fun. Edinburgh has launched the careers of countless comedians, writers and actors who were unknown when they first arrived. Nobody would have chosen them in advance, but audiences discovered them.
An open festival also builds its audience in a different way. At a fringe, people do not simply sit through one long program. They wander from show to show, take a chance on something unfamiliar and tell their friends what they found. Imagine our school grounds with a poetry reading in the library, a band on the basketball court and a science magic show in Lab 3, all running at once.
Critics may worry that some acts will not be polished. They are right; some will not. But a festival is not an exam. Its purpose is to celebrate creativity, and creativity is often messy before it is marvellous. The organisers can still set sensible rules about safety, time limits and suitable content without judging talent.
In 1947, eight groups refused to wait for an invitation. Our school does not have to make its performers wait either. Let's open the doors, hand out a map of venues and see who turns up.

In August 1947, a grand new arts festival opened in Edinburgh, Scotland. Its organisers had invited orchestras, opera companies and famous theatre groups from across Europe. But eight small theatre companies that had not been invited turned up anyway. Rather than going home, they found whatever spaces they could and put on their shows around the edges of the official program. A local writer described their efforts as happening on the 'fringe' of the festival, and the name stuck.
Those uninvited performers started something remarkable. Today, the Edinburgh Festival Fringe is one of the largest arts festivals on the planet, with thousands of shows each August staged in theatres, school halls, cafes, lecture rooms and even a double-decker bus. Its central rule is simple: there is no selection panel. If you can find a venue and pay the registration fee, you can perform.
Australia has embraced the idea. The Adelaide Fringe began in 1960 and is now the largest arts festival in the Southern Hemisphere. During February and March, the city is transformed. Comedians perform in shipping containers, jugglers fill the parks, and a magician might share a laneway with a string quartet.

They wander from show to show, take a chance on something unfamiliar and tell their friends what they found. ComprehensionText:
The Toll of Merrow Bridge
In the valley town of Merrow, the only way across the river was an old stone bridge, and under the bridge lived a troll whose name nobody knew. Nobody had ever asked.
The troll was not cruel, but he was particular. Every traveller who wished to cross had to pay a toll, and the toll was always the same: 'Give me something you have never given anyone before.'
The merchants of Merrow thought this a fine bargain. The goldsmith handed over a ring he had made that very morning. The weaver gave a scarf woven from thread so fine it floated. The mayor, who liked to make an impression, offered a silver cup polished until it shone like the moon. The troll accepted each gift with a heavy nod and stepped aside.
Yet the troll grew no happier. If anything, he grew greyer and more hunched each season, and his treasures piled up in a damp, gleaming heap that he never looked at. Stranger still, the bridge began to crack. Fine lines crept across the stones, then wider ones. The townsfolk muttered that the troll's sour mood was seeping into the bridge itself, for everyone knew that a troll and his bridge share one heart.
'Pay him more,' said the mayor. 'Something truly magnificent.' So the town collected its finest treasures, and still the cracks grew.
One spring morning, a girl named Edda arrived at the bridge with a basket of eggs to sell at the market on the far side. She was the stonemason's youngest apprentice, and she had nothing of value: no rings, no silver, not even a coin.
'Give me something you have never given anyone before,' rumbled the troll.
Edda thought hard. She looked at the eggs, but she had sold eggs a hundred times. She looked at her hands, rough from carrying stone. Then she looked at the troll himself, really looked, at his drooping ears and the moss growing in the creases of his elbows.
'I have never asked anyone their name,' she said, 'because I already know every name in Merrow. But I don't know yours.'
The troll blinked. For a long moment, the only sound was the river.
'Ormund,' he said at last, in a voice like a small stone rolling. 'My name is Ormund.'
'Good morning, Ormund,' said Edda, and she sat down on the bank beside him. She stayed until the market had closed, asking about the river, the fish and the hundred winters he had spent under the arches. She never did sell her eggs. When she finally stood to leave, she noticed that one of the deepest cracks in the bridge had begun to close, like a wound healing over.
Edda came back the next day, and the day after that, bringing her trowel and a bucket of mortar. As they talked, she patched the smaller cracks, and the larger ones mended on their own.
The goldsmith, watching from his window, could not understand it. 'She paid him nothing,' he complained.
The mayor said nothing at all. But the following week, he walked down to the bridge without his silver cup, stood a little awkwardly in front of the troll, and asked him how he was.
QuestionText: What did the goldsmith give the troll?
AnswerA: a scarf of very fine thread
AnswerB: a cup polished like the moon
AnswerC: a ring he had made that morning

ComprehensionText:
Bringing the Whole Clan Together: How to Plan a Family Reunion
Families today are often scattered across suburbs, states and even continents. Cousins may know each other only through photos, and the stories older relatives carry can fade without anyone noticing. A family reunion gathers everyone in one place, but a good one does not happen by accident. The following steps will help you plan a day that people remember for the right reasons.
Step 1: Form a small team. Planning a reunion alone is exhausting. Ask two or three relatives from different branches of the family to help. A mix of ages works best: an older relative will know who should be invited, while a younger one may be quicker at setting up a group chat or an online invitation.
Step 2: Build the guest list. Start with the oldest living generation and work downwards, branch by branch. It is easy to forget second cousins, new partners or relatives who have moved overseas, so ask each branch to check its own section. A shared spreadsheet with names, contact details and ages will save confusion later.
Step 3: Choose a date and place. Give people at least six months' notice, especially if some must travel long distances. School holidays or long weekends usually suit the most people. When choosing a venue, think about who is coming. A park with shelter, toilets and wheelchair access may suit a crowd of toddlers and elderly relatives better than a restaurant, and it is usually cheaper.
Step 4: Share the costs and the food. A 'bring a plate' lunch spreads the work and lets each household contribute a dish it is proud of. If you need to hire a venue or buy supplies, divide the cost fairly and be open about where the money goes. Arguments about money can sour a reunion before it even begins.
Step 5: Plan activities for every generation. Not everyone will want to sit and chat all day. Organise games that mix ages, such as a trivia quiz about family history with teams that include a grandparent, a parent and a child. A 'memory wall' also works well: invite people to pin up old photographs and label who is in them. Some of the best conversations start when a teenager points at a faded picture and asks, 'Who is that?'
Step 6: Record the day. Ask someone to take photos, and consider setting up a quiet corner where older relatives can be recorded telling stories about their childhood. These recordings often become the most treasured part of the reunion, especially in years to come.
Step 7: Follow up. Within a week, send everyone the photos and a thank-you message. Update the guest list with any new contacts. Then ask the big question: when shall we do it again?
A reunion takes effort, but the reward is more than a pleasant afternoon. When three or four generations share a meal and a laugh, children discover that they belong to a story much larger than themselves.

Ahmose Writes Home
This is an imagined letter from a boy training to be a scribe in ancient Egypt, about 3300 years ago.
To my father Senu, at the farm beside the eastern canal, from your son Ahmose, at the scribes' school in Thebes. I hope this finds you well and the fields green.
Father, I have received your message. You say the river rose well this year, that the barley stands thick, and that you want me home for the harvest and home for good after it. I have read your words many times, and now I ask you to read mine.
First, let me tell you how my days pass. We rise early and sit in rows in the courtyard, cross-legged, with our writing boards on our knees. Our teacher, old Paneb, reads a line aloud and we copy it. We do not write on papyrus yet, because papyrus is costly and our mistakes are many. Instead we write on flat chips of limestone and broken pieces of pottery, which are everywhere and cost nothing. When a chip is full, we throw it on the pile behind the wall. That pile is now taller than I am, and I think half of it is mine.
My hand has grown steadier. I mix my own ink now: black from soot, red from ochre, each pressed into a little cake and wetted with water. I chew the end of my reed until it frays into a fine brush. Paneb says my signs are beginning to look like signs and less like ants that have fallen into the ink. From Paneb, who has never praised anyone, this is high praise.
Some days we copy lists: the names of birds, of fish, of towns along the river. Other days we copy old letters and wise sayings, so that we learn good manners as well as good signs. The script we use for everyday writing is quicker than the careful pictures carved on temple walls. Paneb says no granary clerk has time to draw a whole owl for every word.
Now, Father, consider what a scribe can do. A scribe counts the grain in the granaries. A scribe measures the fields after the flood washes away the boundary marks, so that every farmer receives his rightful land. A scribe writes the letters that carry news up and down the river. Who measured our own fields last season? A scribe. Who wrote down how much grain we owed? A scribe. If one of our family could do these things, would anyone ever cheat us again?
I know the harvest is hard and the days are long. I have not forgotten the heat, the dust, the ache in my back after a day with the sickle. I am not running from the work, Father. I am learning a different kind of work, one that can protect the work you do.
Paneb says that if I keep at my lessons for four more years, I may be given a place in the office of the granary. Four years is a long time. But a sycamore is not grown in a single season, and you have told me so yourself.
I will come home for the harvest, as you ask, and I will swing a sickle beside my brothers. But when the barley is in, let me return to my chips of stone and my fraying reed. Send your answer with the boatman who brings this letter.
Your son, who still smells of soot,
Ahmose

First, let me tell you how my days pass. We rise early and sit in rows in the courtyard, cross-legged, with our writing boards on our knees. Our teacher, old Paneb, reads a line aloud and we copy it. We do not write on papyrus yet, because papyrus is costly and our mistakes are many. Instead we write on flat chips of limestone and broken pieces of pottery, which are everywhere and cost nothing. When a chip is full, we throw it on the pile behind the wall. That pile is now taller than I am, and I think half of it is mine.
My hand has grown steadier. I mix my own ink now: black from soot, red from ochre, each pressed into a little cake and wetted with water. I chew the end of my reed until it frays into a fine brush. Paneb says my signs are beginning to look like signs and less like ants that have fallen into the ink. From Paneb, who has never praised anyone, this is high praise.
Some days we copy lists: the names of birds, of fish, of towns along the river. Other days we copy old letters and wise sayings, so that we learn good manners as well as good signs. The script we use for everyday writing is quicker than the careful pictures carved on temple walls. Paneb says no granary clerk has time to draw a whole owl for every word.
Now, Father, consider what a scribe can do. A scribe counts the grain in the granaries. A scribe measures the fields after the flood washes away the boundary marks, so that every farmer receives his rightful land. A scribe writes the letters that carry news up and down the river. Who measured our own fields last season? A scribe. Who wrote down how much grain we owed? A scribe. If one of our family could do these things, would anyone ever cheat us again?
I know the harvest is hard and the days are long. I have not forgotten the heat, the dust, the ache in my back after a day with the sickle. I am not running from the work, Father. I am learning a different kind of work, one that can protect the work you do.
Paneb says that if I keep at my lessons for four more years, I may be given a place in the office of the granary. Four years is a long time. But a sycamore is not grown in a single season, and you have told me so yourself.
I will come home for the harvest, as you ask, and I will swing a sickle beside my brothers. But when the barley is in, let me return to my chips of stone and my fraying reed. Send your answer with the boatman who brings this letter.
Your son, who still smells of soot,
Ahmose
